question: How can public data be used to trace what Spanish political parties actually DO with their public subsidies and campaign money, and to link named politicians to hate-related conduct using only verifiable records rather than inference? Research these angles: (1) What granularity of Spanish party spending is publicly declared and where — Tribunal de Cuentas electoral and annual accounting reports, the fiscalización of gastos electorales, what expense categories are itemised (publicity, mailings, rallies, digital ads), and whether any dataset or API exposes it beyond PDFs. (2) Whether any official Spanish body has formally linked specific party campaign spending, advertising or material to hate speech or discrimination — Junta Electoral Central rulings on campaign content, Fiscalía provincial hate-crime unit prosecutions, court judgments against politicians for hate speech (delitos de odio, art. 510 Código Penal), rulings by autonomous-community equality bodies or LGBTI observatories, and Consejo Audiovisual sanctions. (3) Spain's official hate-crime statistics — the Ministerio del Interior "Informe sobre la evolución de los delitos de odio en España", its methodology, whether it is machine-readable, and any peer-reviewed research examining correlation between political discourse or election campaigns and reported hate crime incidence in Spain or comparable EU states. (4) What per-politician verifiable records exist and can be systematically retrieved: criminal convictions involving hate speech, Fiscalía cases, JEC sanctions, parliamentary disciplinary records, and whether Spanish law and the CGPJ/CENDOJ jurisprudence database allow publishing named individuals' judicial records. (5) How existing trackers and NGOs classify political actors' discourse defensibly — methodologies from ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map, FELGTBI+ and Arcópoli observatorios, Spanish and EU hate-speech monitoring projects, and academic content-analysis of manifestos such as the Manifesto Project — plus the legal and ethical constraints in Spain (LO 1/1982 on honour, GDPR Art. 10 on criminal-conviction data) on publishing a "hateful" label attached to a named living politician.
note: Claims are the union across every resume attempt, deduplicated on the first 160 characters, because the eighteen sources that failed to fetch on the first run were retried and re-extracted. The final run scored 124 claims from its own 26 sources and adjudicated the top 28; stats describes that run. Votes are every adversarial verdict recorded in the journal, so a claim adjudicated across more than one attempt carries more than three.

findings.claim: Angle 1 (party spending granularity, Tribunal de Cuentas, itemised electoral expense categories, dataset/API exposure) produced zero surviving verified claims in this round and remains unanswered.
findings.evidence: Of 18 confirmed claims, none concerns Tribunal de Cuentas, fiscalización de gastos electorales, expense itemisation (publicidad, mailings, mítines, digital ads), or any dataset/API beyond PDFs. The single spending-adjacent verified record is the Junta Electoral de Zona Madrid lona case, which is an electoral-timing infringement, not accounting data. Treat this angle as not researched rather than as a negative result.

findings.claim: Spain channels art. 510 CP hate-crime cases through a formal specialised prosecution structure: a national Fiscal de Sala para los delitos de odio y contra la discriminación with its own substantivity since 1 April 2015, plus Fiscales Delegados in every territorial office and Fiscales de Enlace in area offices.
findings.evidence: Circular 7/2019 FGE (BOE núm. 124, 24 May 2019) records the post created 10 Oct 2011, absorbed 12 Dec 2012 by the Fiscal de Sala de Criminalidad Informática, and from 1 April 2015 existing with its own substantivity; plus designation of Fiscales Delegados territorially and a Fiscal de Enlace in area offices. Strengthened since: unit formally created by RD 311/2023, coordinator appointed by RD 460/2023 (Miguel Ángel Aguilar García), two adscritos by RD 579/2023 and 580/2023, 50 provincial delegados. Ley 15/2022 amended art. 18.3 EOMF to make a hate-crime case register in each Fiscalía Provincial a legal obligation.

findings.claim: That structure is not a machine-readable per-politician data source: its published output is aggregate statistics with anonymised case descriptions, and as of the 2024 reporting year only two internal applications were under development for 2025 (unit case management, and the unified national registry required by art. 18.3 EOMF and art. 36 Ley 15/2022).
findings.evidence: Memoria FGE 2025 cap. III.10.4 describes both applications as entering service during 2025, grounded in the art. 18.3 EOMF obligation created by Ley 15/2022 and art. 36 of that law; Memoria 2024 records the unified-registry work as taking only 'los primeros pasos' in Sept 2023. The sections present statistical tables plus anonymised cases (a victim described only as 'un jugador de fútbol del Real Madrid C. F.'); no defendant is named. FGE also states its hate-crime statistics are compiled manually by provincial specialists for lack of adequate IT tools, and that when affected groups request data on their collective it is often impossible to give a reliable answer. Note: the registries are internal case-management systems, never designed as public datasets, so even once live they do not become a public API.

findings.claim: Official Fiscalía hate-crime volumes for 2024: 477 diligencias de investigación opened (511 in 2023), 293 escritos de acusación (210 in 2023, ~+40%), 173 sentences with 129 convictions (74.5%) and 44 acquittals; most prosecuted offence art. 510.2 a) CP at 162 accusations vs 85 in 2023; motive breakdown of investigations racism/xenophobia 150, sexual orientation/gender identity 93, antisemitism 33, ideology 32.
findings.evidence: Verified directly in Memoria FGE 2025 cap. III.10.4 (§10.4.3.2.1 investigations, §10.4.3.2.2 accusations, §10.4.4 sentences); arithmetic checks (293/210 = +39.5%; 129+44=173; 129/173 = 74.57%). Corroborated by El Independiente 2025-09-05, Servimedia, Público, OBERAXE. Two nuances: 'preprocesal investigations' is a loose rendering of diligencias de investigación incoadas; the memoria tracks 'nación u origen nacional' separately at 127, so the 150 racism figure is not an exhaustive xenophobia total. Accusation-level motive figures differ from investigation-level (racismo/xenofobia 121, orientación/identidad 119, ideología 19) — do not conflate the two datasets.

findings.claim: Spain's official hate-crime statistics are self-declared as a severe undercount: the Ministerio del Interior report states that only one in ten hate-crime victims had reported the offence per the 2021 Encuesta sobre delitos de odio, calls the gap the 'cifra sumergida', and attributes infradenuncia to a warning from the EU Fundamental Rights Agency.
findings.evidence: PDF downloaded and text-extracted: 'aquí no están todos los hechos acaecidos en este ámbito debido a la infradenuncia existente, como ha advertido la propia Agencia de Derechos Fundamentales de la Unión Europea (FRA)' and 'solo una de cada diez personas víctimas de delitos de odio había denunciado'; 'cifra sumergida' appears separately in the report's framing of publishing only the 'cifra conocida'. OBERAXE independently reports ~90% of hate crimes in Spain go unreported. The same caveat recurs in the 2023–2025 editions; the 2025 report records 2,417 hate crimes/incidents, +23.6%, a series high. Consequence for a tracker: this series measures police recording and reporting propensity, not incidence, so it cannot support causal claims about political discourse.

findings.claim: No Spanish court finding attaches a hate-crime label to the Vox 'menas' Madrid campaign poster: Juzgado de Instrucción nº 53 de Madrid archived the case by auto of 29 April 2021, and the Sección Segunda of the Audiencia Provincial de Madrid upheld that on 19 July 2021 holding 'no existe delito de odio ni delito electoral', framing the poster as legitimate ideological-partisan struggle in an electoral contest.
findings.evidence: Confilegal (19 Jul 2021), Telemadrid, TheObjective, Público and eldiario.es corroborate the panel (Sanz Altozano pres., García Sedano, De Urbano Castrillo ponente), the holding and the material (Cercanías poster, 'Un mena 4.700 euros al mes, tu abuela 426 euros de pensión/mes', May 2021 Madrid regional election). Notably the appeal was filed by the Fiscalía together with PSOE, Podemos, Izquierda Unida, the Unidas Podemos coalition and the association 'Progresa' — so even Fiscalía backing produced no adverse ruling. El Español (23 Jan 2023) reports the Tribunal Constitucional refused Podemos's amparo for lack of constitutional relevance, closing the case definitively. Caveats: this is an auto confirming sobreseimiento at instruction stage, not a merits sentencia — correct label is 'case archived; court found no indicia of an art. 510 CP offence', never 'acquitted'; all verification is secondary press and the auto's roll number is unknown, so the primary text should be pulled from CENDOJ/AP Madrid before publication; Libertad Digital (5 Jul 2021) reports an earlier AP Madrid resolution on the same matter, so more than one auto may exist.

findings.claim: Junta Electoral removal orders cannot be cited as official findings of hate or discrimination: the Junta Electoral de Zona de Madrid ordered Vox in June 2023 to remove a campaign lona within one day, but on LOREG art. 53 plus JEC Instrucción 3/2011 (commercially contracted propaganda outside the campaign period), expressly declaring itself not competent to rule on the content's possible illegality and opening no sanctioning file.
findings.evidence: Resolution Monday 26 June 2023 after a PSOE complaint (~22 June) and a parallel complaint by the Asociación Española contra las Terapias de Conversión; lona on a calle Alcalá façade, removed around midday 27 June. 'Plazo de un día' and the art. 53 basis are corroborated across COPE, Telecinco, Servimedia, eldiario.es, Ara, Público, El Plural, Demócrata — politically diverse, so not a press-release artefact. The Junta's stated reasoning: it is not competent to pronounce on content because its remit is limited to the regularity of campaign acts. The competence limit is not a one-off: in the 2021 menas case the Junta Electoral Provincial de Madrid likewise declared itself incompetent on content and referred the complaint to the courts/Fiscalía. Caveats: the deciding body was a Junta Electoral de Zona, not the JEC itself; the primary acuerdo text was not retrieved; JEZ acuerdos are not published in any machine-readable register, so secondary reporting is the practical ceiling. A tracker must label this record as an electoral-timing/advertising infringement only. Separately, adverse content-adjacent orders do exist (Madrid JE ordered withdrawal of a 2023 Vox poster showing a hand throwing an LGBTIQ+ flag into a bin), so the category must not be generalised as 'Juntas never act'.

findings.claim: Verifiable per-politician hate-related judicial records do exist but are individual, staged and press-mediated: the Tribunal de Instancia de València (Sección de Instrucción nº 15) ordered the opening of oral trial against sitting Vox Valencia councillor Cecilia Herrero for hate offences under arts. 510.1 and 510.2 CP, with the Audiencia Provincial de Valencia designated as trial court.
findings.evidence: Five outlets across the political spectrum, 26–27 May 2026 (TheObjective, El Español, Vozpópuli, Valencia Plaza, elperiodic.com/actualidadvalencia.com). Conduct: ~30 tweets Apr 2020–Apr 2024 targeting migrants (Maghrebi/Muslim), LGBTQI+ people, racialised persons and people with disabilities. Fiscalía seeks 3 years prison plus 12 months fine at €20/day plus inhabilitación. Sección Cuarta of the Audiencia Provincial de Valencia dismissed her appeal against the auto de procedimiento abreviado, finding sufficient indicia. Right-leaning outlets reporting adversely on Vox cuts against outlet bias. Hard constraints: this is an auto de apertura de juicio oral — an accusation, so any tracker must label it 'processed / awaiting trial', never 'committed a hate crime'; instruction-phase autos are generally not in CENDOJ, so the record is docketable at the court but not retrievable from the open jurisprudence database; publishing it processes a living person's criminal-proceedings data, engaging GDPR Art. 10 and LO 1/1982.

findings.claim: Supreme Court hate-crime records involving politicians also run the other direction and must not be inverted: the Sala de lo Penal's auto of 29 July 2021 (referencing autos of 8 Nov 2018 and 21 June 2021) archived Vox's querella against Ione Belarra over campaign statements, holding art. 510 CP protects social minorities and not other collectives such as political parties.
findings.evidence: The blog source is weak but the claim does not rest on it: Confilegal (08-09-2021), infolibre and the official CGPJ press note ('El Tribunal Supremo archiva una querella de Vox contra la ministra de Derechos Sociales y Agenda 2030 por delito de odio', ponente Julián Sánchez Melgar) confirm court, parties, statements and date. Statements at a 25 April 2021 Collado Villalba rally during the Madrid Assembly election ('publicidad filofascista', 'nazis, pero ya a cara descubierta'). eldiario.es reports the recurso de súplica rejected, so the auto stands. Two constraints: the finding is negative, so as a per-politician record it documents an archived complaint against Belarra and never hate conduct by her; autos de inadmisión in causa especial are not reliably retrievable from CENDOJ, so the citable text in practice comes from the CGPJ press office, which defeats systematic retrieval. Related but separately refuted in this round: the general propositions that art. 510 never covers political parties and that art. 71.1 CE inviolability structurally bars prosecution both failed verification (0-3) — do not rely on them as doctrine.

findings.claim: CENDOJ cannot serve as a named-politician conviction register: publication of judgments is a CGPJ statutory function (art. 560.1.10ª LOPJ) but limited to 'resoluciones que se determinen', and Reglamento 1/2005 art. 7 conditions treatment and dissemination on data-protection law and LOPJ arts. 234 and 266, with CENDOJ declaring the treatment of judgments to comply with personal-data law as one of its own functions — in practice systematic pseudonymisation of parties' names.
findings.evidence: Art. 560.1.10ª LOPJ (as amended by LO 4/2018 and LO 7/2021, still in force) makes official publication a CGPJ duty but only for resolutions 'que se determinen'; CGPJ's own Jurisprudencia page says it publishes the Tribunal Supremo plus 'una selección creciente' of single-judge resolutions — i.e. not all first-instance judgments, which is where most art. 510 CP convictions sit — and states all published resolutions are anonymised with names substituted and other personal data hidden. Reglamento 1/2005 art. 7 (BOE-A-2005-15939, consolidated, last modified by Pleno acuerdo of 12 Feb 2025, BOE 20 Feb 2025) is the article constituting the CENDOJ channel and expressly conditions treatment and dissemination on data-protection law and arts. 234/266 LOPJ. CENDOJ's technique is substituting real names with randomly assigned archaic given names (Saturnino, Candelaria, Venancio, Eulalia) to avoid collisions in judgments containing up to ~500 identities (Confilegal 2023-05-18; academic treatment in Cano Galán, AEDTSS N119). Contrast: the Tribunal Constitucional does publish party names — a different channel. Note the institutional CGPJ page itself is silent on whether names are removed, pseudonymised or retained and cites neither Reglamento 1/2005 nor LO 3/2018, so it cannot alone settle republication questions. Also note art. 453 LOPJ: only the issuing judicial body can certify the legally effective publication date, not the CENDOJ web copy. Two related propositions were refuted in this round (0-3): that CENDOJ is 'the single institutional retrieval point for named-defendant judgments', and that Reglamento 1/2005 makes CENDOJ a comprehensive rather than selective corpus.

findings.claim: Third-party access to case documents is conditioned and carries an honour/privacy standard inside the CGPJ rule itself: under Reglamento 1/2005 art. 4 the requester must state the cause justifying their interest, the Secretario (now Letrado de la Administración de Justicia) assesses that justification and whether to omit personal data, and where there is no personal and direct interest data must be omitted so as to safeguard intimidad personal y familiar, honor y propia imagen.
findings.evidence: Art. 4.1–4.2 verbatim in the BOE consolidated text (last updated 2025-02-20); art. 5 applies the art. 4.2 criteria to certificaciones and testimonios. Reinforced by LOPJ art. 235 (interés legítimo y directo plus prior disociación, per LO 7/2015), art. 235 bis (dissociation for access to sentencia texts) and art. 236 quinquies (suppression of personal data). The art. 235 bis carve-out making fallo personal data public applies only to a closed list of Hacienda Pública offences (CP arts. 305, 305 bis, 306, and 257/258 where the creditor is the Treasury) and not where the amount was paid before firmeza — art. 510 CP sits outside it. Scoping caveats: art. 4 governs the request-for-copy channel, so 'must justify interest' is not the operative constraint for bulk retrieval of already-published (anonymised) jurisprudence; the honour triad is the express purpose clause of a redaction assessment, not a free-standing veto; it echoes art. 18.1 CE rather than LO 1/1982's civil regime; and the lawfulness of republishing a named person's conviction runs through LOPJ arts. 235 bis/ter, Reglamento 3/2018 CGPJ and GDPR Art. 10 rather than art. 4.2.

findings.claim: The defensible labelling rule for a tracker is ODIHR's: the label must match the evidentiary status of the source record. ODIHR publishes civil-society, IGO and Holy See submissions as 'incidents' and government submissions as 'crimes' precisely because it cannot verify that a reported event met a criminal threshold.
findings.evidence: Methodology page verbatim: cases reported by civil society, IGOs and the Holy See are recorded and published as 'incidents' as opposed to 'crimes', because ODIHR cannot verify whether they can be classified as crimes. Two qualifications that sharpen rather than undercut the transfer: ODIHR's 'crimes' tier attaches to police-recorded data, not convictions — it has no conviction tier — so a tracker distinguishing conviction from accusation from archived complaint is building finer tiers than ODIHR's, which is the right direction; and ODIHR's FAQ warns that state-submitted data do not evidence prevalence and cannot be used for cross-country comparison. Related design proposition refuted in this round (0-3): the claim that ODIHR endorses recording bias motivation without victim/perpetrator demographics as a data-protection-safe pattern — do not cite that.

caveats: Angle 1 is a hole, not a finding: nothing verified about Tribunal de Cuentas electoral or annual accounting reports, itemised expense categories, or dataset/API exposure. Do not treat its absence as evidence that such data is unavailable — it was simply not established here, and must be re-researched before any spending feature is designed. Angles 2 and 4 rest heavily on press-secondary sources for the case-level records (menas archiving, the June 2023 lona order, the Cecilia Herrero trial opening): primary texts (autos, JEZ acuerdos) were not retrieved, roll numbers are unknown, and at least one duplicate-resolution risk was flagged in the menas case. Pull primary texts before publishing any of these. Time-sensitivity: the Fiscalía registry status is scoped to the 2024 reporting year, and today is 2026-09-08, so a Memoria 2026 may report those applications as operational — re-check rather than assert the pipeline is still absent; the Herrero case was at oral-trial-opening in May 2026 and its outcome may have changed. Two independent findings converge on the same structural constraint: CENDOJ pseudonymises party names by design and Fiscalía publishes only aggregates, so there is no route to a systematic named-politician hate-record dataset in Spain — any per-politician record must be assembled case by case from court dockets, CGPJ press notes and press coverage, each carrying its own verification burden. Ten claims were refuted in verification, several of them attractive-sounding doctrinal shortcuts (that art. 510 CP categorically excludes political parties; that art. 71.1 CE inviolability structurally bars prosecution; that Circular 7/2019 requires 'peligro real'; that CENDOJ is a comprehensive corpus or the single retrieval point; that CENDOJ's reuse mandate supports third-party redistribution) — none of these may be relied on. Legal exposure is unresolved rather than cleared: GDPR Art. 10, LOPJ arts. 235 bis/ter, Reglamento 3/2018 CGPJ and LO 1/1982 all bear on publishing a named living politician's criminal-proceedings data, and no verified claim in this round establishes a lawful basis for doing so. Angles 3 (peer-reviewed correlation research between political discourse and hate-crime incidence) and 5 (ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map, FELGTBI+, Arcópoli, Manifesto Project methodologies) were only partly served — the Interior undercount and ODIHR labelling findings landed, but no academic correlation literature and no NGO or manifesto-coding methodology survived verification. Finally, the Interior series measures reporting and police recording, not incidence, so it cannot support any causal or correlational claim linking campaigns to hate crime.
openQuestions: What granularity does the Tribunal de Cuentas actually publish for electoral and annual party accounts — are expense categories (publicidad exterior, mailings, mítines, publicidad digital) itemised per party per election, and does anything exist beyond PDFs (datos.gob.es, an open-data portal, structured annexes)? This angle returned nothing and needs a dedicated re-run.

Has the Fiscalía's unified national hate-crime registry (art. 18.3 EOMF, art. 36 Ley 15/2022) become operational since the 2024 reporting year, and does the Memoria 2026 expose any case-level or per-defendant breakdown — or does it remain internal-only with no public interface?

What is the lawful basis, if any, for publishing a named living Spanish politician's hate-related judicial record — how do GDPR Art. 10, LOPJ arts. 235 bis/ter, Reglamento 3/2018 CGPJ and LO 1/1982 interact where the case is already publicly reported and the person is a public figure, and does prior press notoriety change the analysis?

Are there official Spanish adverse determinations on party campaign content from bodies other than criminal courts and Juntas Electorales — autonomous-community equality bodies, Consejo Audiovisual sanctions, or the Madrid JE's 2023 LGBTIQ+-flag poster withdrawal — and were any of them content-based rather than timing- or format-based?

What per-politician records exist in the parliamentary disciplinary channel (Congreso/Senado/regional assemblies), are they published in a retrievable form, and do they ever characterise conduct as discriminatory in a way a tracker could cite as an official finding?

refuted.claim: Under Circular 7/2019 mere expression of hateful ideas or opinions is not criminal under art. 510 CP: the conduct must generate a real danger (peligro real) to the protected interest, so offensive political discourse cannot be treated as legally equivalent to a hate crime.

The Fiscalía General del Estado states that judicial and prosecutorial IT systems have gaps that make it impossible to produce a global, itemised figure for hate crime, so art. 510 case data exists only as aggregate annual counts — not as a per-case or per-defendant retrievable dataset.

CENDOJ is the CGPJ body created by Article 619 LOPJ that operationally collects, archives, certifies and preserves judgments, so it is the single institutional retrieval point for named-defendant judgments (e.g. art. 510 CP hate-speech convictions).

Reglamento 1/2005 CGPJ (BOE núm. 231, 27/09/2005; consolidated version dated 20/02/2025) mandates that all Juzgados and Tribunales transmit a copy of every sentencia to the CGPJ via the Centro de Documentación Judicial (CENDOJ) — the legal basis for CENDOJ being a systematic, comprehensive corpus of Spanish judgments rather than a selective one.

ODIHR states that strict data-protection law need not block hate-crime recording, because bias motivation of the offender can be recorded without recording the victim's or perpetrator's demographic background — a design pattern applicable to a GDPR/LO 1/1982-constrained tracker (record the recorded conduct and its bias category, not personal characteristics).
The charge is specifically under Código Penal art. 510.1 and 510.2, confirming that the art. 510 route is the operative legal hook for prosecuting politicians' hate speech in Spain.

Art. 510 CP hate-speech protection covers vulnerable minorities defined by protected characteristics (race, ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation, disability), not political parties; so calling a rival party filofascista or nazis is not an art. 510 offence though it may engage honour statutes.

Article 71.1 of the Spanish Constitution grants deputies and senators inviolability for opinions expressed in the exercise of their functions, and the Supreme Court characterises it as absolute, perpetual (surviving loss of office) and non-waivable — a structural bar to prosecuting many parliamentary statements, meaning no conviction record will exist for them.

The JEC page publishes art. 130 as a versioned consolidated text with a validity period rather than as structured data — the version retrieved is marked as in force 01/04/2015 to 01/11/2016 and notes modification by Ley Orgánica 8/1991 — so the legal-definition layer itself must be read as dated HTML/PDF, with no dataset or API exposure.
CENDOJ's mandate expressly includes onward dissemination to publishers for reuse, which supports a legal basis for third parties redistributing CENDOJ judgment content.
