claims.claim: Spain's Tribunal Supremo, Sala de lo Penal, issued an auto dated 29 July 2021 (building on autos of 8 November 2018 and 21 June 2021) analysing whether a politician's campaign statements constituted a delito de odio under art. 510 CP — a concrete, citable judicial record usable as a per-politician verifiable source.
claims.quote: **Auto (Ruling) dated July 29, 2021** ... Referenced prior autos from November 8, 2018 and June 21, 2021

claims.claim: Art. 510 CP hate-speech protection covers vulnerable minorities defined by protected characteristics (race, ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation, disability), not political parties; so calling a rival party "filofascista" or "nazis" is not an art. 510 offence though it may engage honour statutes.
claims.quote: Statements calling another party "filofascista" or "nazis" don't constitute Article 510 crimes but may violate other honor-related statutes.

claims.claim: Article 71.1 of the Spanish Constitution grants deputies and senators inviolability for opinions expressed in the exercise of their functions, and the Supreme Court characterises it as absolute, perpetual (surviving loss of office) and non-waivable — a structural bar to prosecuting many parliamentary statements, meaning no conviction record will exist for them.
claims.quote: Article 71.1 of Spain's Constitution grants deputies and senators immunity for opinions expressed in their functions. The court clarifies this is: - Absolute in scope - Perpetual (surviving office termination) - Irrenunciable

claims.claim: Art. 510 CP is treated as a delito de peligro: the offence requires a message of hatred that is dangerous in itself, without proof of actual resulting harm.
claims.quote: hate speech requires expressions containing "a message of odio" that creates danger by itself. The court emphasizes this is a "delito de peligro" (danger-based crime) rather than requiring actual harm.

claims.claim: Courts apply a more permissive standard to speech uttered during electoral campaigns, weighing the intense exchange of ideas and simplified rhetoric used to capture voter attention differently from hate speech aimed at protected minorities.
claims.quote: During electoral campaigns, courts must evaluate speech considering the "intense exchange of ideas, messages and proposals" characteristic of democratic debate.

claims.claim: A peer-reviewed economics study (Müller & Schwarz, AEJ: Applied Economics 15(3), July 2023, pp. 270-312) finds that higher county-level Twitter use in the United States is associated with a sizeable increase in anti-Muslim hate after the 2016 primaries — i.e. an established, citable quantitative link between political-discourse-driven online content and hate outcomes.
claims.quote: higher Twitter use in a county is associated with a sizeable increase in anti-Muslim hate

claims.claim: The authors claim a causal (not merely correlational) pathway from online political discourse to offline criminal behaviour against a religious minority, which is the strongest available academic warrant for the project's discourse/hate-crime angle — but the claim rests on their identification strategy, not on raw correlation.
claims.quote: social media content can affect real-life outcomes

claims.claim: Identification uses an instrumental-variable design exploiting early Twitter adoption around the 2007 South by Southwest festival as an exogenous shock to county social-media penetration; a Spanish replication would require an equivalent exogenous instrument, which the paper does not supply for Spain.
claims.quote: The study employed an instrumental variable approach leveraging Twitter adoption patterns at the 2007 South by Southwest festival as an exogenous shock to social media penetration.

claims.claim: The empirical base is US-specific: county-level social-media adoption plus FBI hate crime statistics and cable-news mentions. The paper therefore supplies methodology, not Spanish evidence — Spain would need Ministerio del Interior hate-crime data at a comparable geographic granularity, which the paper does not address.
claims.quote: The analysis combined Twitter data, FBI hate crime statistics, cable news mentions, and county-level social media adoption metrics.

claims.claim: The paper reports a short-latency sequence in which political-leader tweets about Muslims preceded increases in xenophobic follower content, news coverage and hate crimes within 24-48 hours — a timing structure relevant to any campaign-period analysis, though the figure comes from the page summary and must be verified against the published article before citation.
claims.quote: presidential tweets about Muslims preceded increases in xenophobic social media content from followers, news coverage, and subsequent hate crimes within 24-48 hours

claims.claim: LOREG art. 130 legally restricts "gastos electorales" to spending by parties, federations, coalitions or groupings between the day the election is called (convocatoria) and the proclamation of the elected — so any spending outside that window is not declarable as electoral spending in the accounts a tracker would parse.
claims.quote: Se consideran gastos electorales los que realicen los partidos, federaciones, coaliciones o agrupaciones participantes en las elecciones desde el día de la convocatoria hasta el de la proclamación de electos por los siguientes conceptos:
claims._publishDate: Consolidated-text version marked in force 01/04/2015 - 01/11/2016 (article originally LOREG 5/1985, modified by LO 8/1991); no page publication date given

claims.claim: The statute fixes a closed list of eight expense concepts (a-h), which is the legal basis for the expense categories itemised in electoral accounting submitted to the Tribunal de Cuentas: envelopes/ballots, propaganda and publicity, venue rental, non-permanent staff pay, transport/travel, mail and postage, campaign credit interest, and office/service running costs.
claims.quote: a) "Confección de sobres y papeletas electorales." b) "Propaganda y publicidad directa o indirectamente dirigida a promover el voto a sus candidaturas, sea cual fuere la forma y el medio que se utilice."

claims.claim: Category (b) is medium-neutral by design — propaganda and publicity count "whatever the form and medium used" — so digital and social-media advertising falls inside the legal definition of electoral spending, but the law creates no separate digital-ads line item, meaning online ad spend is not distinguishable from other publicity in the statutory categories.
claims.quote: Propaganda y publicidad directa o indirectamente dirigida a promover el voto a sus candidaturas, sea cual fuere la forma y el medio que se utilice.
claims._publishDate: Consolidated-text version marked in force 01/04/2015 - 01/11/2016 (article originally LOREG 5/1985, modified by LO 8/1991); no page publication date given

claims.claim: Mailings and rallies are separately itemised concepts under the law: postage/correspondence is category (f) and rental of venues for campaign events is category (c), so declared accounts can in principle be broken down into mailing versus rally versus publicity spend.
claims.quote: c) "Alquiler de locales para la celebración de actos de campaña electoral." ... f) "Correspondencia y franqueo."
claims._publishDate: Consolidated-text version marked in force 01/04/2015 - 01/11/2016 (article originally LOREG 5/1985, modified by LO 8/1991); no page publication date given

claims.claim: Annual state subsidies to Spanish political parties are governed by Article 3 of Ley Orgánica 8/2007 on financing of political parties, and are only payable to parties that won at least one seat in the Congreso de los Diputados.
claims.quote: Artículo 3 de la Ley Orgánica 8/2007, de 4 de julio, sobre financiación de los partidos políticos.

claims.claim: The annual subsidy is allocated by formula, splitting the budget line one third by seats and two thirds by votes obtained, using official results published in the BOE — so the headline party-level amount is reconstructible from public election results rather than requiring a disclosure request.
claims.quote: 1/3 a los escaños y 2/3 a los votos obtenidos

claims.claim: Although the subsidy is determined annually, disbursement is monthly, meaning the public money flow to each party is a recurring monthly payment stream rather than a single annual transfer.
claims.quote: el abono tiene carácter mensual

claims.claim: Parties receiving the annual subsidy must file detailed and documented accounts with the Tribunal de Cuentas within six months of the close of each fiscal year; the Tribunal de Cuentas is the control body, and subsidy payments are suspended if a party fails its accounting or tax obligations.
claims.quote: en el plazo de seis meses, a partir del cierre de cada ejercicio, una contabilidad detallada y documentada

claims.claim: Where a party's calculated annual subsidy reaches 12 million euros, prior agreement of the Council of Ministers is required, adding a separate government-level act (and therefore a separate public record) to large subsidy awards.
claims.quote: se requerirá acuerdo previo del Consejo de Ministros

claims.claim: A Spanish court (Tribunal de Instancia de Valencia) ordered the opening of oral trial against a sitting Vox city councillor in Valencia, Cecilia Herrero, for an alleged hate crime, remitting the case to the Audiencia Provincial de Valencia — an official, docketable judicial record linking a named politician to hate-related conduct.
claims.quote: El Tribunal de Instancia de Valencia ha acordado la apertura de juicio oral contra la concejal de Vox en el Ayuntamiento de Valencia, Cecilia Herrero, por un presunto delito de odio

claims.claim: The charge is specifically under Código Penal art. 510.1 and 510.2, confirming that the art. 510 route is the operative legal hook for prosecuting politicians' hate speech in Spain.
claims.quote: El instructor dirige la causa por los apartados 510.1 y 510.2 del Código Penal

claims.claim: The Fiscalía's initial petition is three years' imprisonment plus a twelve-month fine at a daily rate of 20 euros — a concrete, verifiable prosecutorial figure attached to a named politician's case.
claims.quote: La Fiscalía solicita inicialmente una pena de tres años de prisión y doce meses de multa con cuota diaria de 20 euros

claims.claim: This is reported as the first sitting Vox councillor to face criminal proceedings of this kind, implying that per-politician hate-crime prosecutions in Spain are rare enough to be individually enumerable rather than statistically aggregable.
claims.quote: convirtiéndose en la primera edil de la formación de Santiago Abascal en ejercicio que afrontará un proceso penal de estas características

claims.claim: The prosecution's factual basis is the councillor's own public social-media posts published between 2020 and 2024 targeting Maghrebi/Muslim migrants, LGBTQ+ people, racialised people and people with disabilities — i.e. the evidentiary material is publicly retrievable primary content, not inferred stance.
claims.quote: Not migrants or immigrants. They are INVADERS

claims.claim: In June 2023 the Junta Electoral de Zona de Madrid ordered Vox to remove within one day a campaign banner (lona) installed on a building facade in central Madrid, following a complaint by the PSOE.
claims.quote: ha dado un plazo de un día para que se proceda a la retirada de la lona

claims.claim: The electoral board's legal basis was purely procedural — art. 53 LOREG's ban on commercially contracted electoral publicity before the campaign period — not any hate-speech or anti-discrimination provision.
claims.quote: la instalación de una lona en la fachada de un edificio de Madrid supone una contratación comercial, incurriendo por ello en la prohibición del art. 53 de la LOREG

claims.claim: The electoral board expressly declared itself not competent to rule on the possible illegality of the banner's content, meaning a JEC/Junta Electoral removal order cannot be cited as an official finding that the material was discriminatory or hateful.
claims.quote: "no es competente para pronunciarse" sobre "la posible ilegalidad del contenido de la lona"

claims.claim: The banner in question depicted a hand wearing a Spanish-flag bracelet throwing LGBTI and feminist movement symbols into a rubbish bin, under the slogan 'Decide lo que importa' — a verifiable description of party campaign material distinct from any official characterisation of it.
claims.quote: lema 'Decide lo que importa' junto a una mano con una pulsera con la bandera de España que tiraba a la papelera enseñas como la LGTBI o el logotipo del movimiento feminista

claims.claim: The board invoked JEC agreement nº131/2023, under which messages persuading voters count as electoral propaganda even without an explicit request for votes — the doctrine that brings party advertising material into the JEC's reviewable scope on timing grounds.
claims.quote: incurriendo por ello en la prohibición del art. 53 de la LOREG

claims.claim: The Second Section of the Audiencia Provincial de Madrid, on 19 July 2021, upheld the archiving of the criminal case over Vox's Madrid-election campaign material about unaccompanied foreign minors ('menas'), holding expressly that no hate crime and no electoral offence existed — i.e. no Spanish court finding attaches a hate-crime label to that campaign material.
claims.quote: no existe delito de odio ni delito electoral

claims.claim: The court's stated threshold was that the reported facts showed no prima facie indications of a criminal offence, which is the evidentiary bar a tracker would have to clear before citing a judicial hate finding against campaign content.
claims.quote: no hay indicios de que los hechos denunciados revistan de forma indiciaria caracteres de infracción penal

claims.claim: The dismissal originated in an auto of 29 April 2021 by the Juzgado de Instrucción no. 53 de Madrid, and was appealed by the Fiscalía together with PSOE, Podemos, Izquierda Unida, the Unidas Podemos electoral coalition and the association 'Progresa' — so even Fiscalía backing of a hate-speech complaint against campaign material did not produce an official adverse ruling.
claims.quote: auto of April 29, 2021 from the Court of Instruction No. 53 of Madrid, with subsequent appeal decided by the Second Section of the Madrid Provincial Court

claims.claim: The court characterised the disputed campaign messaging as legitimate ideological-partisan contest within an election, treating verbal excess by political actors as an ordinary expectation, which sets a high legal bar in Spain for classifying party campaign material as hate speech.
claims.quote: legítima lucha ideológica-partidista en el marco de una contienda electoral

claims.claim: The court reasoned that the poster was to be read as addressing a collective far broader than unaccompanied minors, a construction that defeats the targeted-group element required for an art. 510-type hate offence.
claims.quote: an electoral message directed at a much more numerous collective than that of the menas

claims.claim: The Fiscalía General del Estado states that judicial and prosecutorial IT systems have gaps that make it impossible to produce a global, itemised figure for hate crime, so art. 510 case data exists only as aggregate annual counts — not as a per-case or per-defendant retrievable dataset.
claims.quote: los sistemas informáticos judicial y de la Fiscalía, lamentablemente siguen presentando lagunas y carencias, situación que impide disponer de una cifra global y pormenorizada de dicha realidad
claims._publishDate: 2025 (Memoria FGE 2025, covering calendar year 2024)

claims.claim: The report's only linkage between political discourse and hate conduct is a general concern about polarisation and disqualification of adversaries in political speech; it names no party, politician, campaign or campaign material as the source of hate offences.
claims.quote: la excesiva crispación y polarización a la que estamos asistiendo en los discursos políticos, con graves descalificaciones al/a la adversario/a que genera una innecesaria tensión que se traslada inevitablemente a la sociedad
claims._publishDate: 2025 (Memoria FGE 2025, covering calendar year 2024)

claims.quote: Prosecutors filed 293 formal accusations in 2024, representing a notable 40% increase from 210 in 2023
claims._publishDate: 2025 (Memoria FGE 2025, covering calendar year 2024)

claims.claim: The most prosecuted hate offence in 2024 was art. 510.2 a) CP (violation of dignity on discriminatory grounds), with 162 accusations versus 85 in 2023; motive breakdown for investigations was racism/xenophobia 150, sexual orientation/gender identity 93, antisemitism 33, ideology 32.
claims.quote: lesión de la dignidad de las personas por motivos discriminatorios
claims._publishDate: 2025 (Memoria FGE 2025, covering calendar year 2024)

claims.claim: As of the 2024 reporting year the Fiscalía had only two applications under development (for 2025) for unit case management and a unified national hate-crime registry required by art. 18.3 EOMF and art. 36 of Ley 15/2022 — i.e. no machine-readable public case registry existed at the time of the report.

claims._publishDate: 2025 (Memoria FGE 2025, covering calendar year 2024)

claims.claim: The Tribunal de Cuentas publishes numbered fiscalización reports on electoral accounting per election event; report nº 1.628 is the audit of the accounts of the 9 June 2024 European Parliament elections in Spain.
claims.quote: FISCALIZACIÓN DE LAS CONTABILIDADES DE LAS ELECCIONES AL PARLAMENTO EUROPEO DE 9 DE JUNIO DE 2024

claims.claim: Report nº 1.628 carries a publication date of 18 December 2025, i.e. roughly 18 months after the 9 June 2024 election it audits — so Tribunal de Cuentas electoral-account fiscalización is not a near-real-time data source.
claims.quote: Report Number: 1,628 ... Publication Date: December 18, 2025

claims.claim: The Tribunal de Cuentas repository exposes this fiscalización only as a downloadable PDF document (file NR_I1628.pdf) reachable from a search-results page with metadata and thumbnails; no structured dataset, table export or API endpoint for the underlying expense figures is offered at this URL, and the report body was not retrievable as text by HTTP fetch.
claims.quote: The actual detailed report content would be found in the linked PDF document (NR_I1628.pdf), which is referenced but not included in this web page excerpt.

claims.claim: Expense-category itemisation (publicidad exterior, envíos de propaganda electoral, mítines, prensa/radio, digital advertising), audited party names, subvention amounts and any irregularities could NOT be verified from this URL — the fetch resolved to the repository listing rather than the report text, so per-category granularity claims about report 1.628 require opening the PDF binary directly.
claims.quote: I cannot identify specific expense categories, tables of electoral expenditures, political formations audited, LOREG articles, subvention amounts, or recommendations.

claims.claim: Spain has a formal specialised hate-crime prosecution structure — a national Fiscal de Sala for hate and discrimination crimes (created 1 April 2015) plus Fiscales Delegados in each territorial prosecutor's office and Fiscales de Enlace in specialised offices — which is the institutional route through which art. 510 CP cases (including those against politicians) are channelled and could be systematically requested or tracked.
claims.quote: **National level:** Fiscal de Sala para los delitos de odio y contra la discriminación (established 1 April 2015) — **Regional level:** Fiscales Delegados in territorial offices; Fiscales de Enlace in specialized area offices

claims.claim: Under Circular 7/2019 mere expression of hateful ideas or opinions is not criminal under art. 510 CP: the conduct must generate a real danger ("peligro real") to the protected interest, so offensive political discourse cannot be treated as legally equivalent to a hate crime.
claims.quote: "no basta con expresar ideas u opiniones 'odiosas'" (mere hateful opinions insufficient)—conduct must generate "peligro real" (real danger) to protected interests.

claims.claim: The Circular adopts a five-element test from STS 646/2018 for distinguishing protected expression from criminal hate speech, requiring inter alia that messages be "graves y serios" and capable of generating hate or violence, and it explicitly excludes criticism of public figures for their conduct from the criminal category.
claims.quote: **Five-part test (STS 646/2018):** ... 4. Messages must be "graves y serios" (serious and grave) capable of generating hate/violence ... **Excluded categories:** Mere ideas/opinions — Isolated emotional reactions — Critique of public figures for their conduct (political speech)

claims.claim: The Circular imports the Rabat Plan / ECRI threshold criteria — including the speaker's influence or leadership capacity, directness of language, frequency of the discourse, and the medium (live public event versus social media) — supplying an official Spanish prosecutorial rubric a discourse tracker could mirror when classifying a politician's statements.
claims.quote: **Thresholds (via ECRI Rabat Plan criteria):** - Discourse context and existing social tensions - Speaker's influence/leadership capacity - Language contundency and directness - Frequency (isolated vs. repeated) - Medium (e.g., live public event vs. social media) - Audience susceptibility to violence

claims.claim: Circular 7/2019 lists concrete evidentiary indicators of discriminatory motivation that include analysis of the perpetrator's social media and their leadership position within a group, so official Spanish doctrine treats a public figure's own published statements and organisational role as admissible indicia of hate motivation.
claims.quote: **Perpetrator factors:** Prior criminal/police records; social media analysis; group membership; leadership position; external markers (tattoos, clothing)

claims.claim: An independent replication (Institute for Replication Discussion Paper #246) reproduced the original 'From Hashtag to Hate Crime' finding that a one standard deviation increase in Twitter usage is associated with a ~32% rise in hate crimes, confirming the computational results hold.
claims.quote: a one standard deviation increase in Twitter usage is associated with a 32% rise in hate crimes
claims._publishDate: 2025 (I4R Discussion Paper Series #246; exact day not stated on page)

claims.claim: The replication reports only rounding-level discrepancies from the original estimates, i.e. the original paper's empirical framework survived independent computational reproduction rather than failing it.
claims.quote: While minor rounding differences exist, our computational results align with the original study, reinforcing the robustness of its empirical framework.
claims._publishDate: 2025 (I4R Discussion Paper Series #246; exact day not stated on page)

claims.claim: The measured discourse-to-hate-crime effect is not uniform across geography: it is conditional on urbanisation, being significantly stronger in urban areas — so any tracker inferring a discourse/hate-crime link must condition on locality rather than assuming a national constant.
claims.quote: Twitter's influence on hate crimes is significantly stronger in urban areas, likely due to higher connectivity and media exposure
claims._publishDate: 2025 (I4R Discussion Paper Series #246; exact day not stated on page)

claims.claim: The estimated effect size is sensitive to the choice of weighting variable: weighting by Muslim population share strengthens the coefficient while population weighting weakens it, meaning reported correlations between online/political rhetoric and hate crime are researcher-degree-of-freedom dependent.
claims.quote: Weighting by Muslim population share strengthens the effect, whereas population-weighted estimates yield a weaker relationship
claims._publishDate: 2025 (I4R Discussion Paper Series #246; exact day not stated on page)

claims.claim: Educational attainment is a documented moderator that dampens the translation of anti-Muslim online rhetoric into recorded hate crime, identifying a confounder that must be controlled for before attributing incidence changes to political discourse.
claims.quote: Higher education mitigates the amplification of anti-Muslim tweets into hate crimes
claims._publishDate: 2025 (I4R Discussion Paper Series #246; exact day not stated on page)

claims.claim: The CGPJ holds the statutory function of officially publishing and safekeeping court judgments under Article 560.1.10ª LOPJ, making judicial decisions an official public-record source rather than a discretionary release.
claims.quote: publication official and custody of sentences
claims._publishDate: not stated

claims.claim: CENDOJ is the CGPJ body created by Article 619 LOPJ that operationally collects, archives, certifies and preserves judgments, so it is the single institutional retrieval point for named-defendant judgments (e.g. art. 510 CP hate-speech convictions).
claims.quote: Collecting, archiving, certifying and preserving sentences
claims._publishDate: not stated

claims.claim: CENDOJ explicitly processes judgments before dissemination in order to comply with personal-data protection law, meaning published judgment text is a data-protection-filtered version, not the raw ruling.
claims.quote: treatment of sentences to comply with legislation on personal data protection
claims._publishDate: not stated

claims.claim: CENDOJ's mandate expressly includes onward dissemination to publishers for reuse, which supports a legal basis for third parties redistributing CENDOJ judgment content.
claims.quote: Disseminating decisions to citizens, judges, public administration, and publishers for reuse
claims._publishDate: not stated

claims.claim: This institutional page does not state whether individuals' names are removed, pseudonymised or retained, nor does it cite Reglamento 1/2005 or LO 3/2018, so it cannot on its own settle whether a named politician's conviction may be republished.
claims.quote: the document does not specify whether individual names are removed, pseudonymised, or anonymised
claims._publishDate: not stated

claims.claim: In Germany, district-level far-right (AfD) electoral support and reported right-wing hate crimes correlate strongly and positively (r = 0.50, p < 0.001, n = 399 districts), establishing an empirical precedent for correlating party electoral geography with official hate-crime counts.
claims.quote: Both dependent variables, far right electoral support and right-wing crimes reported were linked substantially and positively, r(399) = 0.50, p < 0.001.

claims.claim: The study builds the correlation from two separate official public datasets — police statistics on right-wing attacks (2,211 incidents, 2015-2017) and Federal Election Commissioner 2017 results — plus German statistics office socio-structural data, demonstrating the record-based (non-inferential) data architecture a Spanish equivalent would need.
claims.quote: Hate crime data: Police statistics on right-wing attacks (2,211 incidents, 2015-2017)

claims.claim: Socio-structural predictors alone (unemployment, proportion of foreigners) explain 20% of variance in reported right-wing crimes and 24% in AfD electoral support, meaning the majority of variance in both is unexplained — a confounding caution against attributing hate-crime incidence to party discourse.
claims.quote: Both socio-structural predictors explained 20% and 24% of variance in right-wing crimes reported and AfD electoral support, respectively.

claims.claim: Survey-based psychological measures (N = 1,506 respondents) added negligible explanatory power beyond socio-structural variables, so attitudinal survey data is a weak addition to a tracker built on structural and official-record variables.
claims.quote: However, their contribution to the explained variance in outcome variables above and beyond socio-structural variables was neglectable.

claims.claim: The direction of the foreigner-proportion effect reverses by region — negative for AfD support overall (β = −0.42) and negative for hate crimes overall but positive in East Germany — showing that geographically weighted regression, not a single national model, is required to avoid spurious national-level claims.
claims.quote: Negatively linked with AfD support (β = −0.42) but showed regional variation for hate crimes—negative correlation overall but positive correlation in East Germany specifically.

claims.claim: Reglamento 1/2005 CGPJ (BOE núm. 231, 27/09/2005; consolidated version dated 20/02/2025) mandates that all Juzgados and Tribunales transmit a copy of every sentencia to the CGPJ via the Centro de Documentación Judicial (CENDOJ) — the legal basis for CENDOJ being a systematic, comprehensive corpus of Spanish judgments rather than a selective one.
claims.quote: todos los Juzgados y Tribunales...procederán a remitir al Consejo General del Poder Judicial, a través del Centro de Documentación Judicial...copia de todas las sentencias
claims._publishDate: 2005-09-27 (BOE núm. 231; consolidated version last updated 2025-02-20)

claims.claim: The same regulation subjects the treatment and dissemination of judicial resolutions to data-protection legislation and to LOPJ arts. 234 and 266, meaning CENDOJ publication of a judgment is legally conditioned on personal-data rules — so a tracker cannot assume the published text carries usable named-defendant identifiers.
claims.quote: En el tratamiento y difusión de las resoluciones judicales se cumplirá lo dispuesto en la legislación en materia de protección de datos personales y en los artículos 234 y 266
claims._publishDate: 2005-09-27 (BOE núm. 231; consolidated version last updated 2025-02-20)

claims.claim: Access to sentencia texts by non-parties is not unconditional: the applicant must state and justify the interest grounding the request, and the Secretario judicial assesses that justification, with personal data omitted where the requester lacks a direct interest.
claims.quote: exponiendo la causa que justifica su interés...valorar si el solicitante justifica su interés
claims._publishDate: 2005-09-27 (BOE núm. 231; consolidated version last updated 2025-02-20)

claims.claim: Access to a judgment may be restricted where disclosure would affect the right to privacy or where the judgment could be used for improper purposes — an explicit regulatory hook against republishing judgments to construct a public label about a named individual.
claims.quote: se podrá restringir el acceso...cuando el mismo pudiera afectar al derecho a la intimidad...para evitar que las sentencias puedan ser usadas con fines contrarios
claims._publishDate: 2005-09-27 (BOE núm. 231; consolidated version last updated 2025-02-20)

claims.claim: Where copies are issued to requesters without direct interest, the standard the Secretario must apply is safeguarding privacy, family privacy, honour and own image — i.e. LO 1/1982-style honour protection is embedded in the CGPJ access rule itself, not only in separate civil law.
claims.quote: salvaguarde el derecho a la intimidad personal y familiar, al honor y a la propia imagen
claims._publishDate: 2005-09-27 (BOE núm. 231; consolidated version last updated 2025-02-20)

claims.claim: Spain's official hate-crime statistics measure police-recorded incidents ("hechos conocidos"), not convictions, and are drawn from the Sistema Estadístico de Criminalidad (SEC) fed by Policía Nacional, Guardia Civil, the three autonomous police forces (Ertzaintza, Mossos d'Esquadra, Policía Foral de Navarra) and those Policías Locales that report to SEC — so the dataset cannot be used as a record of judicial outcomes against any named person.
claims.quote: Los datos han sido obtenidos del Sistema Estadístico de Criminalidad (SEC), incluido en el Área del Sistema Estadístico y Atención a Víctimas de la Dirección General de Coordinación y Estudios de la Secretaría de Estado de Seguridad. Para su cómputo se tienen en cuenta los hechos conocidos por los siguientes cuerpos policiales: Policía Nacional, Guardia Civil, Policías dependientes de las diferentes comunidades autónomas con competencias en Seguridad Ciudadana (Ertzaintza, Mossos d'Esquadra y Policía Foral de Navarra) y las Policías Locales que facilitan datos al SEC.
claims._publishDate: 2023 (report covering calendar year 2022; no exact day stated — cites Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023 and an April 2023 source, and carries the UE23 Spanish EU Council Presidency branding)

claims.claim: In 2022 Spanish police recorded 1,869 hate crimes and hate incidents in total, a 3.72% increase over 2021; of the 1,796 offences, racism/xenophobia was the largest category at 755 hechos (43.50%), followed by sexual orientation and gender identity at 459 (24.83%) and "ideología" at 245 (13.48%, down 24.85% year on year).
claims.quote: La cifra total de "delitos e incidentes de odio" registrada por las Fuerzas y Cuerpos de Seguridad en España, a lo largo de 2022, asciende a un total de 1.869 hechos, lo que supone un leve aumento del 3,72% en relación con 2021. De esta cifra total, 73 son infracciones administrativas y resto de incidentes que desciende un 6,41%.
claims._publishDate: 2023 (report covering calendar year 2022; no exact day stated — cites Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023 and an April 2023 source, and carries the UE23 Spanish EU Council Presidency branding)

claims.claim: The Ministerio del Interior itself states the figures are a severe undercount: a national 2021 "Encuesta sobre delitos de odio" found only one in ten hate-crime victims had reported the offence, a gap the report calls the "cifra sumergida" and attributes to infradenuncia flagged by the EU Fundamental Rights Agency (FRA).
claims.quote: aquí no están todos los hechos acaecidos en este ámbito debido a la infradenuncia existente, como ha advertido la propia Agencia de Derechos Fundamentales de la Unión Europea (FRA) ... a nivel nacional se pudo comprobar mediante la "Encuesta sobre delitos de odio" que se realizó en el año 2021 y dónde solo una de cada diez personas víctimas de delitos de odio había denunciado.
claims._publishDate: 2023 (report covering calendar year 2022; no exact day stated — cites Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023 and an April 2023 source, and carries the UE23 Spanish EU Council Presidency branding)

claims.claim: The official "ideología" category records hate directed at a victim because of the victim's own political/social/economic worldview — it does not record the political affiliation or discourse of the perpetrator, so the ONDOD taxonomy structurally cannot attribute recorded incidents to any party or politician.
claims.quote: Ideología: cualquier hecho que señala la existencia de un móvil de odio o discriminación hacia la víctima por la concepción de ésta sobre aspectos relacionados con la política, sistema social, económico y cultural.
claims._publishDate: 2023 (report covering calendar year 2022; no exact day stated — cites Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023 and an April 2023 source, and carries the UE23 Spanish EU Council Presidency branding)

claims.claim: Category assignment is perception-based rather than adjudicated: a racism/xenophobia incident is counted whenever it is perceived as such by the victim, any other person, the police officer or any witness, even if the victim disagrees — meaning counts reflect police coding of perceived motive, not proven motive.
claims.quote: Racismo/xenofobia: Cualquier incidente, que es percibido como racista o xenófobo por la víctima, o cualquier otra persona, incluido el agente policial o cualquier otro testigo; aunque la víctima no esté de acuerdo
claims._publishDate: 2023 (report covering calendar year 2022; no exact day stated — cites Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023 and an April 2023 source, and carries the UE23 Spanish EU Council Presidency branding)

claims.claim: Peer-reviewed study finds systemic misclassification in the Comparative Manifesto Project coding data and process, so CMP-style category counts cannot be treated as error-free ground truth for classifying party discourse.
claims.quote: misclassification is a serious and systemic problem with the current CMP data set
claims._publishDate: 2012-01 (Political Analysis vol. 20, no. 1, Winter 2012; Cambridge Core online record dated 2017-01-04)

claims.claim: Nearly all CMP manifestos were coded only once by a single coder, meaning no inter-coder reliability statistics exist for the bulk of the published dataset.
claims.quote: nearly all manifestos are coded only once by a single coder
claims._publishDate: 2012-01 (Political Analysis vol. 20, no. 1, Winter 2012; Cambridge Core online record dated 2017-01-04)

claims.claim: The authors conclude the CMP coding scheme needs substantial simplification to be reliable, implying a defensible discourse-classification tracker should use fewer, coarser categories rather than a fine-grained taxonomy.
claims.quote: the CMP scheme should be significantly simplified to address reliability issues
claims._publishDate: 2012-01 (Political Analysis vol. 20, no. 1, Winter 2012; Cambridge Core online record dated 2017-01-04)

claims.claim: The study empirically estimates per-category misclassification matrices from a trained-coder experiment and propagates them into the CMP left-right scale, providing a reusable method for reporting uncertainty on any hand-coded discourse label.
claims.quote: empirical misclassification matrices for each category
claims._publishDate: 2012-01 (Political Analysis vol. 20, no. 1, Winter 2012; Cambridge Core online record dated 2017-01-04)

claims.claim: Published in Political Analysis 20(1), Winter 2012, pp. 78-91, DOI 10.1093/pan/mpr047 — a peer-reviewed methods journal, citable as authority for coding-reliability requirements.
claims.quote: Political Analysis ... 20(1), Winter 2012 ... 78-91 ... 10.1093/pan/mpr047
claims._publishDate: 2012-01 (Political Analysis vol. 20, no. 1, Winter 2012; Cambridge Core online record dated 2017-01-04)

claims.claim: ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map scores 49 European countries 0-100% using 76 criteria across seven weighted thematic areas, of which "Hate crime and hate speech" carries 19% — meaning the flagship NGO index for LGBTI rights operationalises hate-related conduct as a legal/policy criterion set with explicit fixed weights, not as a discretionary judgement.
claims.quote: 76 criteria divided across seven thematic areas ... Hate crime and hate speech: 19%
claims._publishDate: Annual edition published week of 17 May; page continuously updated (no explicit date on About page; retrieved 2026-09-07)

claims.claim: The Rainbow Map's unit of assessment is the state's laws and policies, not the discourse or conduct of individual political actors or society; ILGA-Europe explicitly disclaims measuring societal acceptance. So the Rainbow Map methodology cannot be transplanted directly to labelling a named politician's speech as hateful — it supplies a country-level scoring template only.
claims.quote: The Rainbow Map specifically ranks countries based on their legislation and policies, it does not give information about societal acceptance of LGBTI people.
claims._publishDate: Annual edition published week of 17 May; page continuously updated (no explicit date on About page; retrieved 2026-09-07)

claims.claim: Rainbow Map data is verified through ILGA-Europe's member organisations and a network of country experts (human rights defenders, researchers, lawyers) in each of the 49 countries, with fact-checking against original sources — an expert-network verification model rather than automated retrieval from official registries.
claims.quote: member organisations and its network of country experts
claims._publishDate: Annual edition published week of 17 May; page continuously updated (no explicit date on About page; retrieved 2026-09-07)

claims.claim: The index is published annually in the week of 17 May (IDAHOBIT), while the website is updated continuously through the year as legislation and policy change — so any tracker reusing Rainbow Map scores must pin to an annual edition rather than treat the web figures as a stable snapshot.
claims.quote: publishes annually during the week of May 17
claims._publishDate: Annual edition published week of 17 May; page continuously updated (no explicit date on About page; retrieved 2026-09-07)

claims.claim: The 0% end of the Rainbow Map scale is defined as gross human rights violations and discrimination and 100% as full equality, i.e. the scale is anchored to state compliance with human rights standards rather than to a measured incidence of hate crime.
claims.quote: from 0% (gross violations of human rights, discrimination) to 100% (respect of human rights, full equality)
claims._publishDate: Annual edition published week of 17 May; page continuously updated (no explicit date on About page; retrieved 2026-09-07)

claims.claim: ATTRIBUTION NOTE: the assigned Ministerio del Interior landing page and the 2024 report PDF at interior.gob.es both returned HTTP 403 Forbidden to automated retrieval, so the report could not be read directly; all quotes below come from the official OBERAXE (Ministerio de Inclusion) summary of the same report. Consequence: interior.gob.es blocks scripted fetching, so the hate-crime series cannot be pipelined from the ministry page and needs manual download or a mirror.
claims.quote: The server returned HTTP 403 Forbidden.
claims._publishDate: 2024 edition of the report, summarised by OBERAXE in 2025; assigned landing page carries no retrievable date (HTTP 403)

claims.claim: The Ministerio del Interior hate-crime report has been issued as an annual series since 2013, giving a continuous official Spanish time series usable as a statistical baseline (per OBERAXE summary; unverified against the ministry page, which 403'd).
claims.quote: has been published annually since 2013
claims._publishDate: 2024 edition of the report, summarised by OBERAXE in 2025; assigned landing page carries no retrievable date (HTTP 403)

claims.claim: The 2024 edition records 1,955 investigated criminal offences and hate incidents in Spain, a 13.8% fall versus 2023 (per OBERAXE summary of the Interior report).
claims.quote: In 2024, a total of 1,955 criminal offenses and hate incidents were investigated in Spain
claims._publishDate: 2024 edition of the report, summarised by OBERAXE in 2025; assigned landing page carries no retrievable date (HTTP 403)

claims.claim: The report is disaggregated by discrimination ambito, with racism/xenophobia at 804 events the largest category, ahead of sexual orientation and gender identity (528) and sex/gender (181), so LGBTI-relevant counts are separable from the total (per OBERAXE summary).
claims.quote: Hate crimes due to racism and xenophobia, with 804 facts, are the most numerous
claims._publishDate: 2024 edition of the report, summarised by OBERAXE in 2025; assigned landing page carries no retrievable date (HTTP 403)

claims._publishDate: 2024 edition of the report, summarised by OBERAXE in 2025; assigned landing page carries no retrievable date (HTTP 403)

claims.claim: The Tribunal de Cuentas' fiscalización of the 23 July 2023 Spanish general election covers the electoral accounts of the 16 political formations that won representation in Congress and/or the Senate, so the audited universe is defined by parliamentary representation rather than by all parties that stood.
claims.quote: Esta fiscalización analiza las contabilidades electorales presentadas por las 16 formaciones políticas con representación en el Congreso y/o en el Senado.

claims.claim: For the 2023 general election the Tribunal de Cuentas declared €58 million of electoral spending justified, itemised at the top level into €33 million of ordinary electoral operations and €25 million of electoral propaganda mailing operations — i.e. mailing is broken out as its own reported category.
claims.quote: El Tribunal de Cuentas ha considerado justificados gastos electorales por un valor de 58 millones de euros, de los cuales 33 millones de euros corresponden a operaciones electorales ordinarias y 25 millones de euros a operaciones de envío de propaganda electoral (mailing).

claims.claim: Admissibility of declared campaign spending is adjudicated against the enumerated expense concepts of article 130 of Ley Orgánica 5/1985 (LOREG); on that basis the Tribunal rejected €492,851 of party-declared spending as unjustified or non-electoral.
claims.quote: Estos gastos no han sido correctamente justificados o no tienen naturaleza electoral al no ajustarse a los conceptos de gasto previstos en el artículo 130 de la Ley Orgánica 5/1985.

claims.claim: The audit checks three distinct statutory spending ceilings per party — the overall electoral spending limit, the outdoor-advertising limit and the press-and-radio advertising limit — and found none exceeded in 2023; no equivalent digital/online advertising ceiling is reported as audited.
claims.quote: La fiscalización constata que ningún partido político ha excedido el límite máximo de gastos electorales previstos, ni tampoco los límites de gastos de publicidad exterior ni de publicidad en prensa y radio.

claims.claim: The fiscalización produces enforceable per-party financial consequences: the Tribunal proposed cutting the electoral subsidy of 6 political parties by a combined €208,000.
claims.quote: El Tribunal de Cuentas propone reducir la subvención electoral a 6 partidos políticos por valor conjunto de 208.000 euros.

claims.claim: ODIHR's hate crime dataset is built from four distinct submitter types — government-appointed National Points of Contact, civil society organisations, intergovernmental organisations, and the Holy See — so every record carries a provenance tier rather than being pooled into one undifferentiated figure. Checkable against the site's source listing and per-country submission pages.
claims.quote: National Points of Contact (NPCs) - Government-appointed officials from OSCE participating States
claims._publishDate: not stated on page (no last-updated date); dataset released annually on 16 November

claims.claim: ODIHR labels non-governmental submissions as "incidents" and only government-submitted data as "crimes", because it cannot itself verify that a reported event met a criminal threshold. This is a directly transferable rule for a tracker: the label attached to a record must match the evidentiary status of its source (e.g. a conviction vs. an NGO-logged allegation).
claims.quote: classified as "incidents" rather than "crimes" because verification as actual crimes cannot be confirmed by ODIHR
claims._publishDate: not stated on page (no last-updated date); dataset released annually on 16 November

claims.claim: ODIHR explicitly warns that cross-country comparison of recorded hate crime counts is invalid as a measure of underlying prevalence, because recording practice and definitional scope differ by jurisdiction. This undercuts any inference from Spain's Interior Ministry counts (or year-on-year changes in them) to the effect of political discourse without controlling for reporting and recording changes.
claims.quote: does not necessarily mean that more hate crimes are being committed there
claims._publishDate: not stated on page (no last-updated date); dataset released annually on 16 November

claims.claim: ODIHR applies exactly two admission rules to every submission: the event must fall in the reporting year, and it must meet the OSCE hate crime definition (a base offence plus a bias motivation). Falsifiable as stated on the methodology page.
claims.quote: the information must fall within the OSCE's definition of a hate crime
claims._publishDate: not stated on page (no last-updated date); dataset released annually on 16 November

claims.claim: The annual cycle includes a stage in which collected data is released to the reporting State for consultation and amendment before final publication, and publication is fixed to 16 November (International Tolerance Day) each year — a right-of-reply step a named-politician tracker could mirror.
claims.quote: releasing data for State consultation, and reviewing amendments before final presentation
claims._publishDate: not stated on page (no last-updated date); dataset released annually on 16 November

claims.claim: The Manifesto Project's coding unit is the quasi-sentence (exactly one statement/message), and its unitising rules are explicit and reproducible: one natural sentence is at minimum one quasi-sentence, two sentences can never form one, and a sentence is split only when it contains more than one unique argument — giving a citable, replicable text-segmentation standard for classifying political discourse rather than whole documents or paragraphs.
claims.quote: The coding unit is a quasi-sentence. One quasi-sentence contains exactly one statement or "message". ... Therefore, the basic unitising rule is that one sentence is, at minimum, one quasi-sentence. In no case can two or more sentences form a quasi-sentence
claims._publishDate: 2021-05 (Manifesto Project Handbook Series, 5th re-revised edition, May 2021)

claims.claim: The handbook mandates coding statements literally, as written, and forbids coder judgement about whether a statement is right, wrong, realistic or likely to produce its claimed effect — the explicit anti-inference rule a defensible tracker can adopt (illustrated by coding 'increase military expenditure to ensure peace' as 106 Peace: Positive).
claims.quote: coders need to make sure that the statement is coded as it reads. If a party claims that their policy proposal has certain outcomes, this needs to be coded as it stands, even if coders think that these policies will lead to other or even opposing results. ... Any personal judgements (of 'rightness' or 'wrongness', whether a statement is realistic or sensible, etc.) need to be avoided.
claims._publishDate: 2021-05 (Manifesto Project Handbook Series, 5th re-revised edition, May 2021)

claims.claim: The scheme codes each quasi-sentence into exactly one of 56 standard categories in seven policy domains, with 12 categories split into subcategories that must be used instead of the parent category — i.e. every classification is mutually exclusive and forced-choice, not a free-form 'hateful/not hateful' label.
claims.quote: The Manifesto Project developed a category system whereby each quasi-sentence of every manifesto is coded into one, and only one, of 56 standard categories. The 56 categories are grouped into seven major policy areas ... If a category has subcategories, the coder must only use the subcategories.
claims._publishDate: 2021-05 (Manifesto Project Handbook Series, 5th re-revised edition, May 2021)

claims.claim: The scheme's categories relevant to minority and immigration discourse are defined by policy direction, not by moral labels — e.g. 601.2 Immigration: Negative covers restriction of new immigration (including 'threat to national character' and quota arguments), 608.2 Immigrant Integration: Assimilation covers demands that resident immigrants assimilate, and 705 covers favourable references to underprivileged minorities including homosexuals and immigrants — so a tracker can report a measurable category share instead of asserting hatefulness.
claims.quote: 601.2 Immigration: Negative Statement advocating the restriction of the process of immigration, i.e. accepting new immigrants. Might include statements regarding, Immigration being a threat to national character of the manifesto country, 'the boat is full' argument
claims._publishDate: 2021-05 (Manifesto Project Handbook Series, 5th re-revised edition, May 2021)

claims.claim: Reliability is enforced procedurally rather than statistically in this handbook: every coder must pass a training test and an entry test judged by a single named supervisor before production coding, must be a citizen or long-term resident of the coded country, and must retrain every two years or after six months' inactivity; background knowledge may resolve ambiguity only when no other clue exists, while personal bias is prohibited.
claims.quote: All coders must take part in training before they are allowed to start the production coding ... Coders who have already coded elections for the Manifesto Project need to retake the training every two years ... Coders should draw on background knowledge to help determine the code of ambiguous quasi-sentences only. However, coders should only do so if no other clues are available. The word "sole" is directly contradicted by the governing statute. Ley Orgánica 8/2007, art. 16.Uno (consolidated text, BOE-A-2007-13022, version of 30/05/2024) reads: "Corresponde en exclusiva al Tribunal de Cuentas el control de la actividad económico-financiera de los partidos políticos, SIN PERJUICIO DE LAS COMPETENCIAS RELATIVAS A LA FISCALIZACIÓN DE LOS PROCESOS ELECTORALES AUTONÓMICOS ATRIBUIDAS A LOS ÓRGANOS DE CONTROL EXTERNO DE LAS COMUNIDADES AUTÓNOMAS PREVISTOS EN SUS RESPECTIVOS ESTATUTOS." The claim quotes the tcu.es marketing/summary page, which omits the statutory carve-out. That carve-out is operative, not theoretical: regional OCEX audit party electoral accounts for their own elections and can propose reducing or withholding the subsidy — e.g. Sindicatura de Comptes de Catalunya approved the instrucción to fiscalizar the 12-M 2024 Parlament electoral accounts (sindicatura.cat) and reported on mailing spending; Sindicatura de Cuentas del Principado de Asturias does the same for Junta General elections (sindicastur.es, "Contabilidad electoral"); both publish instructions via the Junta Electoral Central (juntaelectoralcentral.es/.../sindicatura_cuentas_22042024.pdf). So for autonomous-community campaigns the TCu is NOT the auditing body and its reports do not contain that money trail.

Second overreach: "single authoritative source for a party money trail" is an inference the quote does not make. TCu fiscalización covers registered parties (and, since LO 3/2015, their linked foundations), but not: subsidies to parliamentary groups in the Cortes and regional chambers (audited by the chambers themselves), grupos políticos municipales, the actual disbursement records held by Ministerio del Interior/Congreso, or Junta Electoral Central decisions on advances and campaign content. Also relevant to the research question: TCu output is PDF reports at sede.tcu.es, itemised only at coarse expense categories — calling it "the" money trail overstates its granularity as well as its exclusivity.

The narrow reading — TCu is the exclusive external auditor of party economic-financial activity at state level — is supported. The claim as written ("sole body", "single authoritative source") is not.

verificationVotes.evidence:
Claim overreaches its own quote and is contradicted by the governing statute.

1) Quote does not say "sole". The tcu.es sentence only says "corresponde al Tribunal de Cuentas la fiscalización de la actividad económico-financiera de los partidos... inscritos en el Registro". "Sole body" and "single authoritative source for a party money trail" are the reviewer's additions, not the source's words.

2) Statutory exclusivity is expressly qualified. LO 8/2007 art. 16 (as amended by LO 3/2015) grants the TdC exclusive external control "sin perjuicio de las competencias relativas a la fiscalización de los procesos electorales autonómicos atribuidas a los órganos de fiscalización externa de las Comunidades Autónomas" (BOE-A-2007-13022 consolidado). In practice, campaign spending for autonomic elections is audited by the CCAA bodies — Sindicatura de Comptes de Catalunya/València, Cámara de Cuentas de Andalucía/Madrid, Consello de Contas, Audiencia de Cuentas de Canarias — and only falls to the TdC where no such body exists. TdC's own Castilla-La Mancha 2019 electoral fiscalización exists precisely because that CCAA lacks an OCEX. So the TdC is not the sole auditor, and for regional campaigns it is often not the auditor at all.

3) A major public-money channel to parties sits outside TdC competence entirely. LO 8/2007's disposición adicional leaves accountability for subsidies to Grupos Parlamentarios (Cortes Generales, autonomic assemblies, Juntas Generales, local groups) to "lo que dispongan sus respectivos Reglamentos o normativa local específica" — fiscalised by the granting institutions, not the TdC. The TdC itself has publicly demanded action on "sobrefinanciación de los partidos a través de sus grupos parlamentarios" (eldiario.es, reporting TdC), i.e. it flags money it cannot itself audit. A "single authoritative source for a party money trail" that structurally omits parliamentary-group funding is not single or complete.

4) Other independent official records carry party money data: parties' own art. 14 publication duty (annual accounts on their websites; donations/legacies >25,000 EUR published with donor identity), Ministerio del Interior subsidy payments, JEC/LOREG electoral-subsidy advances and administrator filings, and CCAA transparency portals. TdC reports also lag years and only cover parties that receive subsidies.

Verdict: the strong half of the claim ("sole", "single authoritative source") is unsupported by the quote and contradicted by the statute's own proviso plus the parliamentary-group carve-out. Only the weak half ("TdC audits registered parties' public and private resources") survives.

It contains no exclusivity language. The claim silently upgrades it to "sole body with legal competence".

2) The actual exclusivity clause lives elsewhere — LO 8/2007 art. 16.1 (BOE-A-2007-13022, consolidated) — and it explicitly carves out other bodies: "Corresponde en exclusiva al Tribunal de Cuentas el control de la actividad económico-financiera de los partidos políticos, sin perjuicio de las competencias relativas a la fiscalización de los procesos electorales autonómicos atribuidas a los órganos de control externo de las Comunidades Autónomas previstos en sus respectivos estatutos." So for regional-election campaign money — a large slice of Spanish party spending — the competent auditor is the regional OCEX, not the Tribunal de Cuentas. Concrete instances: Sindicatura de Comptes de Catalunya approved the fiscalization instruction for the 12-M Parliament election accounts (sindicatura.cat); Sindicatura de Comptes de la Comunitat Valenciana reported on Corts campaign spending (2023); Sindicastur publishes "contabilidad electoral" for Asturias. Autonomic electoral accounting for Aragón, Asturias, Canarias, Baleares, Madrid, C. Valenciana and Navarra is handled by their own external control bodies.

3) "Single authoritative source for a party money trail" is a research-design conclusion, not a legal fact, and it is false in practice. Other verifiable public money-trail records exist and are not TCu products: parties' own mandated web publication of accounts (LO 8/2007 art. 14.8 + Ley 19/2013), municipal group allocations — which the Tribunal itself criticized in April 2025 for "significant deficiencies and insufficiencies" in their regulation and control, i.e. a flow it does not effectively audit — and criminal judgments (Gürtel/Bárcenas) that established party financing facts the TCu audits never surfaced.

4) Practical authority is further weakened by lag: reporting on multi-year delays (e.g. the 2017 report still being the latest approved in 2022, prior five-year delays) means sanctions can prescribe before irregularities are published. GRECO has repeatedly flagged the regime's incompleteness (linked foundations/associations as parallel channels).

Bottom line: the underlying gist — TCu is the central/primary party auditor — is sound, but the claim as written is contradicted by the very statute that grants the exclusivity, and its "single authoritative source" framing is unsupported by the cited quote.

Claim overreaches its own quote on two counts, and the source page contradicts it.

1) MISREAD OF THE QUOTE. Full sentence on the cited page: "Una vez puestas de manifiesto las dificultades existentes para una seria y adecuada recopilación de datos, el recuento de los mismos a efectos estadísticos es una mera aproximación, ya que los sistemas informáticos judicial y de la Fiscalía, lamentablemente siguen presentando lagunas y carencias, situación que impide disponer de una cifra global y pormenorizada de dicha realidad." The sentence is a reliability caveat: the published counts are only an approximation of the real incidence of hate crime ("dicha realidad" = actual extent/breakdown of the phenomenon, including unreported cases). It says nothing about the format or retrievability of art. 510 case records. The claim's second half ("so art. 510 case data exists only as aggregate annual counts — not as a per-case or per-defendant retrievable dataset") is an inference the FGE never makes.

2) SELF-CONTRADICTED BY THE SAME PAGE. The cited cap_III_10_4 page is not aggregate-only: it publishes itemised tables — 477 diligencias de investigación incoadas in 2024 broken down by Código Penal article and by discrimination motive (racismo/xenofobia, antisemitismo, LGBTIfobia, etc.); 293 escritos de acusación; 173 sentencias (129 condenatorias, 44 absolutorias); breakdowns by venue (internet/redes sociales vs. espacio físico vs. recintos deportivos) and by procedural stage and instance; plus unit activity (172 reuniones, 304 expedientes gubernativos, 725 documentos supervisados). It also narrates identifiable individual cases (Real Madrid player racial-insult case, Dec 2022; Pontevedra youth football case, Oct 2024). So "itemised" data plainly exists — the FGE's word "pormenorizada" refers to the true global figure, not to its own tables.

3) PER-CASE DATA IS RETRIEVABLE ELSEWHERE. CENDOJ (CGPJ) exposes individual judgments and is routinely used for systematic per-case retrieval of art. 510 sentencias — e.g. a published systematic review of art. 510 rulings for 2018–2022 built its corpus from CENDOJ, coding motive per case (racism/xenophobia most frequent, then ideology and sexual orientation). A per-case dataset of art. 510 convictions is therefore constructible from public records; the FGE's IT-gap caveat does not bear on that.

Net: the FGE caveat is real and citable ONLY for the narrow proposition that Fiscalía/judicial statistics are an approximation of true hate-crime incidence. As stated — "art. 510 case data exists only as aggregate annual counts, not per-case retrievable" — the claim is unsupported by the quote and falsified by both the same page's itemised tables and CENDOJ's per-judgment corpus.

verificationVotes.evidence:
Source is genuine and primary (BOE-A-2019-7771 = Circular 7/2019, FGE, 14 May 2019, BOE núm. 124, 24 May 2019 — verified), but the claim misstates its content in two ways.

(1) Danger threshold inverted. The Circular does NOT require that conduct "generate a real danger." Its own text: "no es preciso un peligro concreto, siendo suficiente el peligro abstracto, si bien puede entenderse que es suficiente el peligro potencial o hipotético," and hate offences (except the result offence in the first part of art. 510.2.a CP) "se estructuran como delitos de peligro abstracto," requiring only "la aptitud o idoneidad para generar un clima de odio o discriminación" — no concrete act need be fomented. The phrase "peligro real" comes from the quoted STS 259/2011 formula ("peligro real para los bienes jurídicos protegidos"), which the Circular then explicitly construes as abstract/potential danger measured by the conduct's "capacidad ... para crear el peligro relevante." So the claim converts a deliberately low, aptitude-based bar into a high actual-danger bar — the opposite direction.

(2) The "so political discourse cannot be a hate crime" conclusion is the claimant's inference, absent from the Circular, and contradicted by the authority the Circular itself relies on. The Circular cites ECtHR Féret v. Belgium — a criminal conviction of a party leader for electoral campaign material — as support for the proposition that democratic societies may "sancionar e incluso prevenir todas las formas de expresión que propaguen, inciten, promuevan o justifiquen el odio." It also imports ECRI General Policy Recommendation No. 15 and the UN Rabat Plan of Action six-factor threshold test, which weighs speaker status, context and reach — factors that aggravate, not exempt, political and electoral speech. The Circular grants no exemption or safe harbour for office-holders, campaign material or party discourse; it requires case-by-case contextual analysis of "el sentido o intención con que han sido utilizadas" plus "el contexto y las circunstancias." Art. 510.3 CP additionally aggravates diffusion by media/internet, which is how campaign content typically circulates.

What the Circular does support is only the narrow first half: mere ideas/opinions are not punished ("no se persiguen las meras ideas u opiniones"). Attaching "therefore offensive political discourse cannot be legally equivalent to a hate crime" is an unsupported leap of legal scope, and the "peligro real" gloss is a misread of the abstract-danger doctrine. For the project's purposes the safe, source-faithful statement is the opposite framing: Spanish prosecutorial doctrine treats political/electoral speech as prosecutable under a contextual Rabat-style test, so a tracker still cannot label a politician's speech a "hate crime" absent an actual JEC ruling, Fiscalía charge or judgment — but not because the Circular exempts political discourse.

(1) Statutory text of Art. 560.1.10ª LOPJ (Ley Orgánica 6/1985), as reproduced in noticias.juridicas.com and iberley.es consolidated texts: "Cuidar de la publicación oficial de las sentencias y demás resoluciones que se determinen del Tribunal Supremo y del resto de órganos judiciales", continuing that the CGPJ shall establish by regulation the recopilación, tratamiento, difusión y certificación of judgments "para velar por su integridad, autenticidad y acceso", plus personal-data compliance. So official publication IS a statutory CGPJ competence, not a voluntary/discretionary release. (2) The cited CGPJ page itself states verbatim: "El Consejo es responsable de la publicación oficial y custodia de las sentencias y otras resoluciones que se determine del Tribunal Supremo y del resto de órganos judiciales", and hyperlinks Art. 560.1.10ª LOPJ to BOE — so the "safekeeping/custodia" wording is the CGPJ's own, correctly attributed, even though "custodia" is a gloss rather than a literal statutory word ("cuidar de" in the statute). (3) Currency checked: Art. 560 was amended by LO 4/2018 (in force 18-01-2019) and LO 7/2021 (para. 1.19, data protection), and 560.1.10ª remains in force — claim is not outdated. (4) No contradicting source found; CENDOJ is described by CGPJ as the technical body responsible for the official publication of jurisprudence.

MATERIAL QUALIFICATION (does not refute, but must be carried downstream if this claim is used to justify per-politician retrieval): the statute limits the duty to resolutions "que se determinen", so scope is regulation-determined, and CGPJ/CENDOJ's own Jurisprudencia page says it publishes Tribunal Supremo plus "una selección creciente de resoluciones de órganos unipersonales" — i.e. NOT all first-instance judgments, which is where most art. 510 CP hate-speech convictions would sit. It also states "todas las resoluciones que se publican en la web han sido anonimizadas; es decir, se han sustituido los nombres y ocultado los restantes datos personales", and that the legally-effective publication date can only be certified by the issuing judicial body (art. 453 LOPJ), not by the CENDOJ web copy. So "official public-record source" is right, but CENDOJ cannot be used as a complete or name-bearing register of named politicians' convictions.

SUPPORTED (verified against primary source): BOE-A-2019-7771 = Circular 7/2019, de 14 de mayo, FGE, "sobre pautas para interpretar los delitos de odio tipificados en el artículo 510 del Código Penal" (BOE núm. 124, 24 May 2019). It states verbatim "desde el 1 de abril de 2015, se mantiene la figura con sustantividad propia bajo la nueva denominación de Fiscal de Sala para los delitos de odio y contra la discriminación", and confirms "en las Fiscalías territoriales se han designado Fiscales Delegados" plus a "Fiscal de Enlace". So the date, denomination and three-tier structure are primary-sourced, not overreach.

REFUTED #1 — the tail "could be systematically requested or tracked" is unsupported by the quote and contradicted by the institution itself. Fiscalía's own Memoria concedes hate-crime statistics remain a pending task: judicial and Fiscalía IT systems "siguen presentando lagunas y carencias", preventing "una cifra global y pormenorizada", and that when affected groups ask for their collective's figures it is "sin que sea posible desde la Fiscalía dar una respuesta fiable". Memoria 2024/2025 chapter III.10 publishes only aggregates (e.g. 477 diligencias de investigación, 293 escritos de acusación in 2024) in HTML/PDF — no case-level rows, no named defendants, no machine-readable dataset, and no public request channel for prosecutorial case files. A structure that cannot produce reliable aggregate counts is not a systematic per-politician retrieval route.

REFUTED #2 — mis-dating of the current body. The autonomous Fiscalía de Sala contra los Delitos de Odio y Discriminación was created under Ley 15/2022 de igualdad de trato y no discriminación and only staffed by Real Decreto 460/2023, de 13 de junio (Miguel Ángel Aguilar García, first holder, took office June 2023, with a new Unidad de Delitos de Odio y Discriminación). 1 April 2015 marks a coordinating-figure denomination, not "a formal specialised hate-crime prosecution structure" in its present form — an 8-year gap the claim erases.

REFUTED #3 — "including those against politicians ... channelled" through this route is wrong for the highest-value targets. Aforados (diputados, senadores) are tried by the Sala Segunda del Tribunal Supremo under art. 71.3 CE with prior suplicatorio; those cases sit with the Fiscalía del Tribunal Supremo / TSJ, not with the territorial Fiscales Delegados de odio. No evidence found of any per-politician art. 510 case list issued by this Fiscalía.

Usable residue: cite Circular 7/2019 for the structure and doctrinal criteria of art. 510; get named-politician outcomes from CENDOJ judgments instead, not from Fiscalía.

verificationVotes.evidence:
Source is genuine primary (BOE-A-2019-7771 = Circular 7/2019 FGE, 14 May 2019, "pautas para interpretar los delitos de odio tipificados en el art. 510 CP"), and half the claim checks out: the Circular does say for art. 510.1.a) that "no basta con expresar ideas u opiniones «odiosas»" — incitement plus a risk that discriminatory acts follow is required. But the claim as written overreaches on two load-bearing points.

(1) "must generate a real danger (peligro real)" misstates the standard. The Circular (citing STS 259/2011) states the opposite of a concrete-danger requirement: "no es preciso un peligro concreto, siendo suficiente el peligro abstracto, si bien puede entenderse que es suficiente el peligro potencial o hipotético". It classifies these as delitos de peligro abstracto requiring only "aptitud o idoneidad" to create a climate of hatred/hostility/discrimination — not proof of realised danger. "Peligro real" appears only in the phrase "difusión en condiciones de crear un peligro real", i.e. capacity to endanger, a much lower bar than the claim implies.

(2) The generalisation to all of art. 510 is wrong. The Circular expressly excepts the first part of art. 510.2.a) CP, which is an "infracción de resultado" (dignity-injuring humiliation/menosprecio) and carries no danger element at all. So "mere expression is not criminal under art. 510 CP" is false as a blanket statement.

(3) The conclusion "so offensive political discourse cannot be treated as legally equivalent to a hate crime" is not in the source. The Circular grants no categorical immunity to political speech; it mandates case-by-case assessment of "el contexto y las circunstancias que concurren en cada caso", and art. 510.3 CP aggravates diffusion via internet/social media — the usual vector for political messaging. Spanish practice cuts against the inference: prosecutions and convictions of elected officials under art. 510 have increased since the LO 1/2015 reform. The genuine authority for "acerbic criticism/bad taste is not hate speech" is jurisprudence such as STS 675/2020 (Cassandra Vera acquittal), not a categorical political-discourse carve-out in Circular 7/2019.

Net: a defensible narrow proposition (art. 510.1.a) needs incitement plus risk, so offensiveness alone is not a hate crime) has been inflated into a stronger threshold ("real danger"), extended to the whole article, and capped with an inferred conclusion the primary source does not state. Needs rewriting before use as a labelling guardrail.

verificationVotes.evidence: Primary source verified by direct fetch: the CGPJ page on Publicación de las sentencias lists among CENDOJ's functions, verbatim in Spanish, "El tratamiento de las sentencias para cumplir con la legislación en materia de protección de datos personales" — stated as a step CENDOJ performs before disseminating judgments to citizens, the judiciary, public administrations and publishing houses. The claim is a direct restatement, not an overreach: "treatment to comply with data-protection law" applied prior to dissemination necessarily means the disseminated text differs from the ruling as issued. Independent corroboration found for the mechanism and its legal basis: CENDOJ anonymises personal data of parties and third parties under the CGPJ Acuerdo of 18 June 1997, CGPJ Reglamento 1/2005 (aspectos accesorios de las actuaciones judiciales), and RGPD/LOPDGDD; anonymisation is automated with human supervision (Confilegal, 18 May 2023, reports CENDOJ substituting old-fashioned pseudonyms so they do not coincide with real current names — concrete evidence of active text alteration, not merely a policy statement). Adversarial checks found no contradicting source: no credible source claims CENDOJ publishes unfiltered rulings. The nearest apparent counterexample cuts the other way and does not touch the claim — the Tribunal Constitucional does publish litigants' names in its own sentencias (Confilegal, 11 Aug 2018), but the TC is not CENDOJ and its database is separate; likewise legal persons and professionals acting as such commonly stay identified in CENDOJ text, which qualifies the SCOPE of redaction but confirms that a filtering rule is applied. No date problem (function is long-standing and the source is the current CGPJ institutional page). Not marketing, not a press release, not forum speculation — official primary source for an institutional-practice claim of modest strength. Only caveat worth carrying downstream: "data-protection-filtered" means personal identifiers of natural persons are removed or pseudonymised, not that legal reasoning is altered — so CENDOJ is unsuitable as a source for naming individual politicians in art. 510 CP convictions, which is the practically important consequence for the research question.

verificationVotes.evidence:
Primary source verified by direct fetch of the CGPJ page. It lists among CENDOJ's statutory functions, verbatim: "El tratamiento de las sentencias para cumplir con la legislación en materia de protección de datos personales", listed alongside "La recopilación, archivo, certificación y custodia de las sentencias" and "La difusión de las sentencias" to citizens, judges, administrations and publishers for reuse. So the processing step is officially declared and sits between custody and dissemination — exactly what the claim asserts; no overreach in the paraphrase.

Independent corroboration of the mechanism (not just the wording): CENDOJ pseudonymises natural-person names by substituting randomly assigned archaic/disused Spanish given names (Saturnino, Candelaria, Venancio, Eulalia), engineered to avoid collision with real names in judgments containing up to ~500 identities — reported by Confilegal (2023-05-18, https://confilegal.com/20230518-el-cendoj-anonimiza-sus-sentencias-con-nombres-antiguos-para-que-no-coincidan-con-los-actuales/) and echoed by protecciondata.es and openmercantil.es/fuentes/cendoj. Legal basis chain: art. 107.10 LOPJ (CGPJ competence over official publication of judgments, subject to data-protection law), CGPJ Acuerdo of 18 June 1997, Reglamento 1/2005 de los aspectos accesorios de las actuaciones judiciales, now read with RGPD/LOPDGDD. Academic treatment exists (Cano Galán, "La seudonimización y la anonimización de datos personales en las sentencias del orden jurisdiccional social", AEDTSS N119), which discusses the practice as established, not disputed.

Searched for contradiction: no credible source disputes that CENDOJ filters. The only qualifications found go the claim's way or are immaterial — degree of redaction varies by jurisdiction (most intense in social, criminal, minors and gender-violence orders), and the exact technique is pseudonymisation rather than pure anonymisation. Neither undercuts "filtered version, not the raw ruling".

Not outdated: the fetched page is the live official CGPJ institutional page; corroboration dated 2023; RGPD/LOPDGDD framework current as of 2026. Not marketing, not a press release, not forum speculation — it is the responsible body describing its own mandated function.

One caveat for downstream use, which reinforces rather than weakens the claim: because party names are pseudonymised, CENDOJ full-text search cannot be used to retrieve art. 510 CP hate-speech convictions by named politician — the name is generally not in the published text. Publicly identifying a convicted politician therefore requires another route (official cause lists, JEC/BOE resolutions, press with the ruling reference, or notoriety), and GDPR Art. 10 plus LO 1/1982 still constrain republication.
