Attempted refutation failed on all five checklist axes.

1) Quote vs claim: no overreach. The CGPJ's own institutional page on "Publicación de las sentencias" lists CENDOJ's functions as the "recopilación, tratamiento, difusión y publicación" chain and explicitly includes "el tratamiento de las sentencias para el cumplimiento de la legislación sobre protección de datos personales" — i.e. processing sits between custody and dissemination to citizens, judges, administrations and publishing companies. The claim asserts exactly that ordering and consequence (published text is a data-protection-filtered version). Fetched page confirms: functions = "Collection, archiving, certification and custody of sentences; Processing judgments for compliance with data protection laws; Distribution to citizens, judges, public administrations, and publishing companies."

2) Contradicting evidence: none found; independent sources reinforce. CENDOJ applies anonymisation of parties' and third parties' personal data per the CGPJ Acuerdo of 18 June 1997 plus RGPD/LOPDGDD; publication in CENDOJ occurs after anonymisation (protecciondata.es "¿Por qué anonimizar las sentencias?"; openmercantil.es CENDOJ source page). Statutory backing is stronger than the claim needs: LOPJ art. 235 bis conditions access to judgment text on "disociación" of personal data, with restriction where privacy, specially-protected persons, or victim anonymity are at stake. Peer-reviewed/doctrinal treatment of pseudonymisation vs anonymisation in published social-jurisdiction judgments (Cano Galán, AEDTSS n.119) discusses the same filtering as an established practice, disputing its adequacy — not its existence.

3) Source quality: primary and authoritative — poderjudicial.es is the CGPJ itself, the body that owns CENDOJ (LOPJ art. 619; publication mandate art. 560.1.10ª LOPJ). Claim strength is modest and institutional, matched by an institutional primary source.

4) Currency: framework is current — LOPJ arts. 235 bis/ter (235 ter added by LO 10/2015) plus RGPD/LOPDGDD 3/2018 all post-date and reinforce the practice; nothing indicates repeal or reversal.

5) Not marketing/press release/forum speculation — it is a statutory-function description on an official institutional page.

Caveat, not a refutation: the CGPJ page does not detail the anonymisation methodology, and the search-note correction is worth carrying forward — the operative rules are LOPJ art. 235 bis/ter + CGPJ agreements + RGPD/LOPDGDD, not "Reglamento 1/2005". For the project's downstream use this matters: CENDOJ text cannot be relied on to carry a named living politician's identity, so per-politician judicial records must be sourced from the ruling's own publicity (art. 235 ter, tax-fraud convictions only) or from press/official communiqués, not scraped names in CENDOJ.

verificationVotes.evidence:
Quote supports only the first half; the load-bearing second half is contradicted, including by the cited page itself.

1) "created by Article 619 LOPJ" is wrong on chronology. CENDOJ was created by the CGPJ in 1997 (HQ inaugurated in San Sebastián 16 Jul 1997); Art. 619 LOPJ and the CGPJ Plenary Agreement of 18 Sep 2003 approving its Reglamento came later. Art. 619 regulates/defines CENDOJ as an "órgano técnico" with functions of "selección, ordenación, tratamiento, difusión y publicación de información jurídica legislativa, jurisprudencial y doctrinal" — it did not create the body. The cited page itself grounds the CGPJ competence in Art. 560.1.10ª LOPJ, not 619.

2) "single institutional retrieval point for named-defendant judgments" is refuted by CENDOJ's own publication regime. The same source page states CENDOJ performs "tratamiento de las sentencias para cumplir con la legislación de protección de datos". In practice every resolution in the CENDOJ search engine is dissociated/pseudonymised under LOPDGDD 3/2018 and the 1997 CGPJ Acuerdo: party names are REPLACED with substitute forenames (documented practice of using archaic names — Saturnino, Candelaria, Venancio, Eulalia — precisely so they cannot be matched to real persons; Confilegal, 18 May 2023: "El CENDOJ anonimiza sus sentencias con nombres antiguos para que no coincidan con los actuales"). Protection is described as especially intense in penal matters — exactly the art. 510 CP hate-speech category the claim invokes. So CENDOJ is structurally the WRONG tool for named-defendant retrieval, not the canonical one.

3) "single" is also false: certified copies of judgments come from the issuing court/LAJ under LOPJ art. 235-266; Tribunal Constitucional rulings are published in the BOE; commercial databases (Aranzadi, La Ley, vLex) receive the CENDOJ reuse feed; and the CGPJ/TS communication office publishes notable judgments separately. The cited page explicitly describes distribution "to citizens, judges, public administrations, and publishing companies for reuse" — a multi-channel model, not a single point.

4) The supporting quote ("Collecting, archiving, certifying and preserving sentences") says nothing about named defendants or about being the single retrieval point. Those are inferences appended to the quote, i.e. overreach — and the direction of the inference is inverted relative to reality.

Net: the descriptive first clause is fine; the operational conclusion a tracker would rely on ("use CENDOJ to pull named art. 510 CP convictions") is false and would produce anonymised judgments with no usable politician identity.

verificationVotes.evidence:
Claim splits into a supported half and an unsupported half; the load-bearing half fails.

SUPPORTED: Art. 619 LOPJ does create CENDOJ as a CGPJ technical body, and the cited page's own wording confirms the function list — "La recopilación, archivo, certificación y custodia de las sentencias para velar por su integridad, autenticidad y acceso" (poderjudicial.es, Publicacion-de-las-sentencias). So "collects, archives, certifies, preserves" + art. 619 is accurate.

REFUTED (the operative conclusion):
1. Quote overreach. The supporting quote says nothing about exclusivity or about named defendants. Fetch of the cited page confirms it "does not claim CENDOJ is the sole or exclusive source" of judgments. "so it is the single institutional retrieval point for named-defendant judgments" is pure inference bolted onto a function list.
2. Legally contradicted on "named-defendant". The same page lists a second function the claim silently drops: "El tratamiento de las sentencias para cumplir con la legislación en materia de protección de datos personales." Art. 235 bis LOPJ requires prior DISSOCIATION of personal data as a condition of access to sentence texts; CGPJ practice (Acuerdo 18-VI-1997, Reglamento 1/2005) anonymises natural persons in the public buscador (poderjudicial.es/search). So CENDOJ's public retrieval channel is precisely NOT a source of named-defendant judgments — an art. 510 CP conviction retrieved there arrives with the defendant's name stripped. Naming a politician from a CENDOJ hit generally requires an external identification step (press, BOE, party records), which is the inference the project's honesty rules forbid.
3. "Single" is false regardless. Other institutional retrieval points exist and are not CENDOJ: Tribunal Constitucional's own jurisprudence database, BOE, the ECLI/e-Justice national case-law portals, court/TSJ press offices (which publish named resolutions in notas de prensa), and the Registro Central de Penados (named but non-public). Library/institutional guides routinely list CENDOJ as one of several free official jurisprudence sources, not the only one.
4. Coverage gap. CENDOJ's mass is collegiate-court resolutions (TS, AN, TSJ, AP); first-instance juzgado de lo penal judgments — where many art. 510 CP prosecutions end — are unevenly present, so even anonymised retrieval is not exhaustive.

Practical consequence for the research question: CENDOJ is a valid starting point for the TEXT of art. 510 CP jurisprudence, but cannot be cited as the mechanism for linking a NAMED politician to a conviction. GDPR Art. 10 / art. 235 bis LOPJ cut exactly there.

verificationVotes.evidence:
Source is genuine and current: BOE-A-2019-7771 = Circular 7/2019, de 14 de mayo, FGE, "sobre pautas para interpretar los delitos de odio tipificados en el artículo 510 del Código Penal", BOE núm. 124, 24 May 2019, pp. 55655-55695. No evidence it has been superseded (still cited as vigente; Memoria FGE 2020 cap. III.12.2 applies it). So not outdated, not marketing.

However the claim overreaches on two points.

(1) Scope error: the "no basta con expresar ideas u opiniones odiosas / peligro real" requirement is the Circular's reading of the art. 510.1 incitement modalities, which it classes as abstract-danger offences ("aptitud o idoneidad para generar un clima de odio, hostilidad, discriminación o violencia"; risk is "real, aunque potencial", i.e. potential/hypothetical suffices — NOT concrete danger). The Circular expressly excludes one modality from that structure: "Los delitos de odio se configuran como delitos de peligro abstracto, con la única excepción de la infracción de resultado tipificada en el primer inciso del art. 510.2.a) CP." So under art. 510.2.a first inciso (humillación, menosprecio, descrédito against a protected group) the offence is a delito de lesión of dignity, where no peligro real to a further protected interest must be shown. The claim's blanket "under art. 510 CP" contradicts the Circular's own carve-out.

(2) Non-sequitur in the conclusion: nothing in the Circular exempts political discourse. It applies favor libertatis and case-by-case weighing (context, audience, emisor's influence, severity), and the emisor's public relevance is a factor weighing toward, not against, criminality; it also states "la libertad de expresión no puede situarse por encima de la dignidad de otro ser humano". Politicians have in fact been convicted under the incitement provision (e.g. AP Barcelona/Manresa, 11 Nov 2011, Plataforma per Catalunya councillor, 1.5 years for incitement to hatred/discrimination/violence; TS 675/2020 sets the balancing test rather than an exemption). "Offensive political discourse cannot be treated as legally equivalent to a hate crime" is therefore only true in the weak sense "merely offensive/insulting speech, absent aptitude to generate the proscribed climate, is not art. 510.1 conduct" — it is false as a categorical statement about political speech.

Survivable narrower version: per Circular 7/2019, art. 510.1 requires more than expressing hateful ideas — conduct apt to create a real though potential risk of the proscribed climate — so a project cannot label discourse a "delito de odio" without a judicial or prosecutorial determination; art. 510.2.a humiliation is the exception and needs no such danger showing.

Three independent defects; the second is fatal for the claim's stated use case (retrieving named art. 510 CP hate-speech convictions).

(1) Legal-attribution overreach. The quoted four functions ("Recopilación, archivo, certificación y custodia de las sentencias") appear on the cited CGPJ page, but that same page grounds them in **art. 560.1.10ª LOPJ** (the CGPJ's competence over official publication and custody of judgments), not art. 619. Art. 619 LOPJ defines CENDOJ's mission in different terms — "la selección, la ordenación, el tratamiento, la difusión y la publicación de información jurídica legislativa, jurisprudencial y doctrinal" (confirmed via poderjudicial.es "El Cendoj, Misión y estructura"). The claim welds a 560.1.10ª function list onto a 619 citation. Imprecise conflation, not a quote-supported statement.

(2) FATAL: CENDOJ is precisely NOT a source of *named-defendant* judgments. The same cited page states CENDOJ performs "tratamiento de las sentencias para cumplir con la legislación en materia de protección de datos personales." In practice this is systematic pseudonymisation: names, surnames, addresses, ID numbers and contact data of parties and third parties are stripped under the CGPJ Acuerdo of 18 June 1997 and Reglamento 3/2010 on reutilización de sentencias (BOE-A-2010-17860), with real names replaced by randomly assigned archaic substitutes (Saturnino, Candelaria, Venancio, Eulalia) explicitly so no real person can be matched — documented by Confilegal, 18 May 2023, "El CENDOJ anonimiza sus sentencias con nombres antiguos para que no coincidan con los actuales." Anonymisation is described as especially intense in penal, social, minors and gender-violence matters — i.e. exactly the art. 510 CP category. So you cannot retrieve or confirm a named politician's hate-speech conviction from CENDOJ by defendant name; the claim's operative purpose is unachievable through that channel.

(3) "Single institutional retrieval point" is false on coverage. poderjudicial.es documents that CENDOJ publishes all resolutions of *colegiado* bodies (TS, AN, TSJ, AP) but only "una selección de las resoluciones de los juzgados unipersonales", chosen by the judges themselves as of "interés jurídico relevante" — so first-instance criminal convictions (Juzgados de lo Penal, where many art. 510 CP cases terminate) are only selectively present. The CGPJ's own guidance directs users of missing judgments to request them "directamente al órgano que la dictó acreditando ser parte o tener interés legítimo" — a separate, non-CENDOJ, interest-gated route. The Tribunal Constitucional maintains its own database, and criminal-conviction records live in the Registro Central de Penados (non-public). Multiple retrieval points, not one.

Source quality is adequate (primary CGPJ page), but it does not say what the claim says — and the anonymisation regime it does mention contradicts the claim's core assertion.

verificationVotes.evidence:
Core claim verified against primary/statutory text, not just the CGPJ marketing page.

1) Statute exists and says this. LOPJ Art. 560.1.10ª (text as reformed by LO 4/2013): "Cuidar de la publicación oficial de las sentencias y demás resoluciones que se determinen del Tribunal Supremo y del resto de órganos judiciales", continuing that the CGPJ "previo informe de las Administraciones competentes, establecerá reglamentariamente" the recopilación, tratamiento, difusión y certificación of judgments "para velar por su integridad, autenticidad y acceso, así como para asegurar el cumplimiento de la legislación en materia de protección de datos personales." Confirmed independently of the cited CGPJ page via https://www.iberley.es/legislacion/articulo-560-ley-organica-poder-judicial and BOE/JEC consolidated LOPJ text. Predecessor provision was Art. 107.10 LOPJ, so this is a renumbering, not a new/soft competence — claim is current (Art. 560 still in force; Reglamento 1/2005 last amended by CGPJ Pleno agreement of 12 Feb 2025).

2) "Safekeeping" is supported, though it comes from the implementing layer rather than the article itself. The word "custodia" does NOT appear in Art. 560.1.10ª. It appears in the CGPJ's own description of CENDOJ's task — "recopilación, archivo, certificación y custodia de las sentencias para velar por su integridad, autenticidad y acceso" — and the article's "integridad, autenticidad y acceso" wording is the statutory hook for it. CENDOJ's mandate is separately statutory (LOPJ Art. 619). So "publishing and safekeeping" is a fair paraphrase, not an invention.

3) "Official public-record source rather than a discretionary release" survives, because "cuidar de la publicación oficial" is a duty imposed on the CGPJ, not a faculty. No credible source found disputing that Art. 560.1.10ª assigns this function.

Qualifications the downstream research must carry (these narrow the claim's usefulness but do not falsify it):
- Scope is bounded by "que se determinen": the statute mandates publication of the resolutions that are *determined* (by CGPJ regulation), not of every judgment. CENDOJ's public jurisprudence database is a selection, so "all judgments are public records" would be an overreach the claim itself stops short of.
- Access is not raw. Art. 560.1.10ª expressly subordinates the regime to data-protection law, and CENDOJ publishes only after disociación/anonymisation — names of natural persons substituted, other personal data hidden, per Reglamento 1/2005 and LO 3/2018. Consequence for the project's angle (4): CENDOJ cannot be used to retrieve *named* politicians' hate-speech convictions; the statutory publication duty does not create a named-individual judicial-record source. Any per-politician conviction linkage needs a different route (press-published Supreme Court/TSJ rulings, CGPJ press office notes on cases of public interest, or the parties' own filings), and still faces GDPR Art. 10 and LO 1/1982 limits.

Verdict: claim as written (statutory function under 560.1.10ª; official rather than discretionary) is well supported by primary law and current. Refutation attempt fails.

The mandate's existence must not be cited as proof of corpus completeness.

The second sentence ("directly transferable rule for a tracker") is a normative design inference, not an empirical assertion, and is a sound analogy — but one imprecision should be carried forward: ODIHR's higher-evidentiary tier is police-RECORDED hate crime, not conviction. Independent reporting (Crónica Global 29/08/2022; HayDerecho 07/07/2022 "Del limitado acceso a las resoluciones judiciales"; a tuderechoasaber.es FOI request specifically on "Criterio de inclusión de sentencias en el CENDOJ") confirms CGPJ sources concede not 100% of resolutions are published and Juzgados de Primera Instancia are effectively absent.

Two further overreaches: (a) Art. 7 governs internal remission to CGPJ, not what is exposed in the public buscador — reception ≠ retrievability, and the claim silently equates them; (b) Art. 7 itself is not unconditional even on its face — only "sentencias" are blanket, other resolutions are filtered by "puedan resultar de interés".

Consequence for the research question: for systematically retrieving named politicians' art. 510 CP convictions, the corpus is precisely selective where it matters — most art. 510 first-instance convictions are Juzgado de lo Penal sentencias, i.e. órgano unipersonal, i.e. discretionary inclusion. Plus published texts are anonymized/pseudonymized under CGPJ/AEPD criteria, so the database cannot be relied on to name individuals. Treating CENDOJ as comprehensive would produce silent false negatives ("no conviction found" read as "no conviction exists").

Primary source confirms the descriptive core almost verbatim. hatecrime.osce.org/our-methodology states: "Cases reported by civil society, IGOs and the Holy See are recorded and published as 'incidents' as opposed to 'crimes'" and "This is because ODIHR cannot verify whether incidents reported by civil society groups can be classified as crimes." The page also states "Civil society incidents are not necessarily comparable to officially recorded hate crimes" and, on the reasons for divergence, "they may not have been verified by the state authorities... some incidents are only reported to civil society groups and not to the authorities, or because different monitoring definitions might be used." So the source/label-alignment convention is real, primary-sourced, and current (page live; 2024 report published Feb 2025). Not marketing, not a press release, not a benchmark, not outdated.

TWO QUALIFICATIONS THAT MUST BE CARRIED FORWARD, one of which makes the claim's illustration wrong as written:

1. The parenthetical "(e.g. a conviction vs. an NGO-logged allegation)" misstates ODIHR's actual line. ODIHR's "crimes" tier is "the number of hate crimes officially recorded" — i.e. police/state-recorded data submitted by government National Points of Contact, NOT convictions. ODIHR reports prosecutions and sentences as separate fields precisely because recording, prosecution and conviction are distinct stages. The real evidentiary ladder is three-tier (NGO report / officially recorded / adjudicated conviction), and the claim collapses it to two. Transferred uncorrected to the Spanish tracker this licenses exactly the error the project must avoid: treating a Fiscalía case opened, a JEC ruling, or a police-recorded incident as equivalent to an art. 510 CP conviction. That distinction is also legally load-bearing under GDPR Art. 10, which covers criminal-conviction data specifically.

2. ODIHR does not verify government submissions either — it publishes what state NPCs submit. The distinction rests on a state authority having applied a legal classification, not on ODIHR having established the facts. The page even warns "The figures do not show the prevalence of hate crime and cannot be used to compare between countries or bias motivations." So the transferable rule is "label = the classification authority that produced the record," not "label = what ODIHR verified to be true."

3. Sentence 2 ("directly transferable rule") is the analyst's normative inference, not an ODIHR statement. It is defensible and transparently framed as an application, so not an overreach that kills the claim — but it should not be cited as an ODIHR recommendation.

Not refuted: the load-bearing principle (label must match the evidentiary status of the producing source) is what ODIHR demonstrably does, on a primary source, currently. Use it, but replace the conviction/allegation example with the three-tier ladder.

Source verification PASSES for the quote, FAILS for the inference that makes the claim useful.

1) Quote is authentic and verbatim. Fetched https://cdn.osce.org/sites/default/files/f/documents/3/a/124533.pdf (301 redirect from osce.org), extracted with pdftotext. Document = OSCE/ODIHR, "Hate Crime Data-Collection and Monitoring Mechanisms: A Practical Guide", ODIHR 2014, ISBN 978-92-9234-895-3. The text sits in "Box 5: Data protection", p. 17-18, exactly as quoted: "Even in states with strict data-protection laws, police can record the bias motivation of the offender(s) without having to record the background of the victim or perpetrator." So the first half of the claim ("ODIHR states...") is fully supported.

2) The second half is an overreach that mis-maps the legal constraint. Box 5's stated problem is narrow and explicit: "data-protection laws that prohibit the gathering and publishing of demographic information relating to victims and suspects... may restrict authorities' powers to record the ethnicity or religious affiliation of a victim". That is a GDPR Art. 9 special-category problem about VICTIM/SUSPECT demographics in POLICE statistics. The constraints named in the claim are different ones: GDPR Art. 10 governs criminal-conviction and offence data, and LO 1/1982 protects the honour of a named living person. Neither is triggered by victim/perpetrator ethnicity or religion; both are triggered by publishing conduct or judicial data attached to a NAME. The claim's prescription — "record the recorded conduct and its bias category, not personal characteristics" — therefore offers no cover for the actual risk in a named-politician tracker, because the recorded conduct tied to a name IS the Art. 10 / LO 1/1982 datum. The pattern is inverted relative to the constraint it is said to solve.

3) Scope mismatch: ODIHR addresses what state police may RECORD, not what a third party may PUBLISH about identified individuals. The guide is in fact hostile to publication on the very same page (p. 17, immediately preceding Box 5): unconfirmed demographic data "would be inappropriate to publish... or to use them as a basis for policy-making". Box 5 is also anchored to MC Decision No. 9/09 (Annex B), a commitment addressed to participating States' data collection, not to civil-society trackers.

4) Additional qualification: ODIHR's own later output and FRA's hate-crime recording work treat bias-motivation-only recording as a floor, not a sufficient design (they push for disaggregation with safeguards), so citing Box 5 as an affirmative design template for a publishing tracker is at minimum heavily qualified.

Net: the attribution is accurate and the source is primary and authoritative, but the operative inference — that this is "a design pattern applicable to a GDPR/LO 1/1982-constrained tracker" — is unsupported by the quote and addresses the wrong legal provision. Not usable as stated.

Quote verified verbatim, but the claim's operative half is an unsupported extrapolation.

VERIFIED PART: pdftotext of the PDF (OSCE/ODIHR, "Hate Crime Data-Collection and Monitoring Mechanisms: A Practical Guide", Warsaw 2014, ISBN 978-92-9234-895-3, p.18, "Box 5: Data protection") contains exactly: "However, it is important to note that data-protection laws need not restrict efforts to record key hate crime data. Even in states with strict data-protection laws, police can record the bias motivation of the offender(s) without having to record the background of the victim or perpetrator." So clause 1 of the claim is accurate attribution.

REFUTATION 1 — subject substitution. Box 5 is about POLICE recording in state criminal-justice statistics ("police can record"), i.e. a competent authority producing aggregate counts. The claim converts it into "a design pattern applicable to a GDPR/LO 1/1982-constrained tracker" — a private publisher attaching a bias label to a NAMED living politician. Nothing in the source addresses third-party publishers, named individuals, or Spanish law. That bridging sentence appears nowhere in the document.

REFUTATION 2 — it solves the wrong legal problem. ODIHR's carve-out drops the DEMOGRAPHIC background (ethnicity/religion — GDPR Art. 9 special-category data) of victim and perpetrator, while keeping the offence+bias category. A named-politician tracker's actual constraints are (a) GDPR Art. 10: processing data "relating to criminal convictions and offences" is lawful "only under the control of official authority or when the processing is authorised by Union or Member State law" (mirrored by Spain's LOPDGDD 3/2018; Art. 10 also confines comprehensive conviction registers to official authority), and (b) LO 1/1982 honour/defamation. Recording "the recorded conduct and its bias category" against an identified politician IS Art. 10 offence data about that data subject — precisely the exposure ODIHR does not discuss. The pattern removes the one element the tracker cannot remove (the identified person) and removes it from the wrong side (victim demographics).

REFUTATION 3 — the same source cuts against publication. One page earlier (p.17) the guide says demographic data based on police perception "would be inappropriate to publish these data, or to use them as a basis for policy-making", and it endorses publication only of official aggregate statistics. Citing it as authority for publishing individual bias labels inverts its posture.

REFUTATION 4 — anachronism. The guide is dated 2014, predating GDPR (applicable 2018), Directive (EU) 2016/680 (LED, the instrument that actually governs police bias-motivation records), and LOPDGDD 3/2018. It therefore cannot be authority on what a "GDPR-constrained" design may do; FRA's 2018 "Hate crime recording and data collection practice across the EU" is the post-GDPR treatment and likewise addresses state authorities, not private trackers.

NET: the bare attribution survives; the claim as written (a transferable design pattern legitimating a GDPR/LO 1/1982-constrained named-politician tracker) is an overreach the quote does not carry.

verificationVotes.evidence:
First clause checks out; second clause is an overreach and is inverted relative to current statute law.

VERIFIED PART: Reglamento 1/2005 CGPJ (BOE-A-2005-15939, still in force, last modified by CGPJ Acuerdo of 12 Feb 2025) art. 4 does require a written request to the Secretaría "especificando el documento o documentos cuyo conocimiento se pretende" and "exponiendo la causa que justifica su interés", resolved by the Secretario within two days, who "deberá valorar si el solicitante justifica su interés, la existencia de derechos fundamentales en juego y la necesidad de omitir datos de carácter personal", with denial reviewable by the Juez/Presidente within three days. So "not unconditional + interest must be stated and assessed" is supported.

REFUTED PART 1 (misstatement of the data-omission trigger): the claim says personal data is omitted "where the requester lacks a direct interest". Current LOPJ art. 235, as worded by LO 7/2021 de 26 de mayo (in force 16 June 2021), says the opposite structure: "El acceso a las resoluciones judiciales, o a determinados extremos de las mismas, o a otras actuaciones procesales, por quienes no son parte en el procedimiento y acrediten un interés legítimo y directo, podrá llevarse a cabo previa disociación, anonimización u otra medida de protección de los datos de carácter personal…". Direct legitimate interest is a PRECONDITION of non-party access, and dissociation/anonymisation applies to that access even when the interest IS accredited — it is not a penalty for lacking one. The "no acrediten interés legítimo → previa disociación" formulation the claim paraphrases belongs to the superseded pre-2015 wording (old LOPJ art. 266.1 / art. 235 bis introduced by LO 7/2015, later restructured); art. 235 bis and 235 ter today deal with publication of firm tax-fraud convictions (LO 10/2015), not with generic sentencia access.

REFUTED PART 2 (source hierarchy / staleness): the cited quote is from a 2005 CGPJ reglamento, subordinate to the LOPJ, and predates LO 7/2015, LOPD 3/2018, LO 7/2021 and LO 1/2025; it still names the "Secretario judicial", a post renamed Letrado de la Administración de Justicia by LO 7/2015. Citing it as the operative rule for a 2026 tooling decision is outdated on both the actor and the anonymisation test.

REFUTED PART 3 (materially misleading for the research question): access to sentencia texts is in fact unconditional through the other official channel — CENDOJ's buscador del Poder Judicial publishes anonymised full judgment texts to any member of the public with no interest justification whatsoever. The claim, unqualified, would wrongly tell a builder that judicial-record retrieval requires per-case justified interest, when only certified copies/testimonios from the oficina judicial do.

Net: the interest-justification procedure exists (Reglamento 1/2005 art. 4), but the claim's second half is unsupported by its own quote and contradicted by LOPJ art. 235 (LO 7/2021), and it omits the open CENDOJ channel that the app would actually use.

Fetched the PDF (osce.org 301-redirects to cdn.osce.org; extracted with pdftotext -layout, saved at C:\Users\ASUS\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--politician-tracking-app\edbf7013-653f-463d-8cfc-071041b61e22\scratchpad\odihr.txt). Document = "Hate Crime Data-Collection and Monitoring Mechanisms: A Practical Guide", OSCE/ODIHR 2014, ISBN 978-92-9234-895-3. The sentence appears verbatim at p.17, inside "Box 5: Data protection" (odihr.txt lines 957-974). So attribution is sound.

REFUTATION 1 — scope mismatch; the claim's second clause is the researcher's inference, not ODIHR's. Box 5 is exclusively about POLICE recording of VICTIM/SUSPECT DEMOGRAPHICS for aggregate statistics. Its opening framing: "Some states have strict data-protection laws that prohibit the gathering and publishing of demographic information relating to victims and suspects... data-protection laws may restrict authorities' powers to record the ethnicity or religious affiliation of a victim". Grep of the full text returns ZERO hits for "named individual", "publish...name", "conviction data", "anonymis/anonymiz". ODIHR says nothing about public trackers, nothing about publishing identified individuals, and nothing about LO 1/1982.

REFUTATION 2 — the pattern does not relieve the constraint the claim says it relieves. A tracker naming living Spanish politicians is constrained by GDPR Art. 10 (personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences) plus Art. 6 lawfulness and LO 1/1982 (honour). None of those turn on whether victim demographics are recorded. Recording "politician X — art. 510 conviction — bias category anti-LGBTI" is Art. 10 personal data about X whether or not any demographic field exists. Worse, ODIHR's own wording is "police can record the bias motivation of THE OFFENDER(S)" — applied to a named politician, the person carrying the bias attribution IS the data subject, so the pattern inverts rather than reduces the risk; and a bias category attached to a named person can itself reveal political opinions/religious or philosophical beliefs, engaging Art. 9. Omitting victim demographics protects third-party victims; it buys the tracker nothing on its actual exposure.

REFUTATION 3 — pre-GDPR and used across a regime change. Grep for "gdpr|2016/679|95/46|general data protection" in the full text: NONE. It is a 2014 document written against pre-2018 national law; citing it as a "design pattern applicable to a GDPR/LO 1/1982-constrained tracker" extrapolates a 12-year-old police-statistics observation onto a legal regime it never analysed.

REFUTATION 4 — the same document actively cautions against publication, cutting against the tracker use. p.17: police-perception demographic data "should only be used for internal intelligence purposes... it would be inappropriate to publish these data". The guide's posture is restrictive about publishing, not permissive.

NET. Salvageable narrow version: "ODIHR (2014) says police can record bias motivation without recording victim/perpetrator demographic background, so strict data-protection law is not per se a bar to hate-crime STATISTICS." The claim as written adds an applicability conclusion ODIHR never drew and which misidentifies the binding constraint on a named-politician tracker.

1. Wrong procedural weight. This is an auto de apertura de juicio oral (case referred to the Audiencia Provincial de Valencia) — an indictment on "indicios racionales de criminalidad", NOT a conviction. An un-adjudicated first-instance charging decision cannot "confirm" any legal proposition; it only shows a judge accepted the qualification. No sentencia exists.

2. The source's own framing contradicts "operative". The headline is "Un juez procesa por PRIMERA VEZ a una concejal de Vox en ejercicio por delito de odio" — i.e. rarity/novelty, not an established route. A first-ever indictment is evidence the route is seldom used against sitting politicians, the opposite of what the claim infers.

3. Directly contradicted for the largest class of Spanish politicians: art. 71.1 CE inviolabilidad parlamentaria bars prosecution of diputados/senadores for opinions expressed in the exercise of their functions (see interjuez.es, "Delito de odio, inviolabilidad parlamentaria y debate político"). Art. 510 is therefore precisely NOT the operative hook for parliamentary speech; this case only proceeds because a municipal concejal enjoys no inviolability. Aforamiento further changes the forum for MPs. Claim as worded is false as a generalisation.

4. Art. 510 is not the only route. Politicians' discriminatory/offensive speech is also prosecuted under art. 578 CP (enaltecimiento/humillación a víctimas), art. 525 CP (escarnio de sentimientos religiosos), and art. 173.1 (integridad moral) — the latter expressly discussed alongside 510.2.a) in the doctrinal literature (Dialnet cod. 8576896, "Delito de odio del artículo 510.2.a) CP ... Integridad moral"). Non-criminal routes (JEC, Consejo Audiovisual) exist too.

5. Source quality mismatch. For a general statement about Spanish criminal-law practice, the primary authority is FGE Circular 7/2019 (BOE-A-2019-7771, pautas para interpretar los delitos de odio del art. 510) plus TC/TS jurisprudence that has narrowed 510 (real-risk requirement), not one partisan-leaning digital outlet's report of one pre-trial decision. TC/TS narrowing also means indictment ≠ conviction, so "operative" is unproven even on the merits.

Net: safe to state "in this case the instructor charged under art. 510.1 and 510.2 CP"; not safe to state that this confirms art. 510 as the operative hook for politicians generally. Cite Circular 7/2019 for the doctrinal point and flag art. 71.1 CE as the limiting condition.

The claim also drops 510.3 (aggravation for internet/social-media diffusion), 510.5 (inhabilitacion especial) and 510.6, which are the subsections that actually drive the penalty and the disqualification from public office — the most research-relevant part. The Objective's one-line summary ("dirige la causa por los apartados 510.1 y 510.2") is itself the imprecise secondary rendering; the claim inherits and hardens that error.

The same article's own headline frames it as "por primera vez" (first sitting Vox councillor processed for delito de odio). A first-of-its-kind, untried prosecution of one municipal councillor cannot "confirm" a general proposition about the operative route for prosecuting politicians in Spain. It evidences one instruction judge's qualification, nothing more.

(3) The general proposition is also an over-simplification, though independently supportable from better sources than this one. Art. 510 is not the only hook for politicians' hate-related speech: art. 22.4 CP (discriminatory-motive aggravating circumstance attached to an ordinary offence), art. 173.1 (degrading treatment), art. 578 (humiliation of terrorism victims — the route in the well-known artist/politician speech cases), art. 525 (religious feelings), and arts. 511/512 (denial of public service/professional discrimination). For aforados (diputados/senadores) prosecution runs through the Sala Segunda del TS with suplicatorio, a hurdle absent for a concejal — so this case does not generalise to "politicians" as a class. Supreme Court and doctrine also narrow 510.1 sharply (provocation must be "directa, concreta, terminante... y grave", excluding mere descalificaciones), and FGE Circular 7/2019 exists precisely because the qualification is contested — i.e. 510 is contested terrain, not a settled "operative hook".

What survives: the narrow fact that this Valencia case is being prosecuted under art. 510 CP subsections is verified by two independent sources. Usable as "one pending art. 510 prosecution of a sitting councillor, charged under 510.1.a) alternatively 510.2.a), plus 510.3/.5/.6, trial pending" — not as confirmation that art. 510 is "the" route.

verificationVotes.evidence:
Claim's legal premise is factually wrong on the statutory text. Art. 510.1 CP lists protected motives as "motivos racistas, antisemitas, antigitanos u OTROS REFERENTES A LA IDEOLOGÍA, religión o creencias, situación familiar, ... etnia, raza o nación, origen nacional, sexo, orientación sexual o identidad sexual, razones de género, aporofobia, enfermedad o discapacidad" (BOE consolidated text; confirmed via Iberley/BOE Circular 7/2019 rendering). "Ideología" — i.e. political ideology — is an EXPRESS protected characteristic, and aporofobia was added by LO 8/2021; the claim's enumeration ("race, ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation, disability") omits the very category at issue.

Contradicting authority, not just omission: FGE Circular 7/2019 (BOE-A-2019-7771) states the art. 510 victim list is a CLOSED list that includes ideology, and expressly holds that assault on, or incitement to hatred against, a person or group of Nazi ideology CAN fall within art. 510 — the opposite of "political groups are outside art. 510". Spanish case law applies 510.2.a) to "ataques ideológicos por motivos políticos" (Diario La Ley case note). Interior's own "Informe sobre la evolución de los delitos de odio" tracks "ideología" as a standing statistical category (241 incidents in 2025, +64%; 58.2% fall in 2024), which would be impossible if ideology were not a protected motive.

Source quality mismatch: a strong doctrinal assertion about the scope of a criminal statute is sourced only to a 2021 law blog (interjuez.es), with no cite to statute or STS/STC. The quote is also weaker than the claim built on it — the quote asserts a case-level outcome ("filofascista/nazis statements don't constitute 510 crimes"), while the claim generalises it into a categorical rule about what art. 510 covers.

What survives: the practical conclusion may often hold, but for a different reason — Circular 7/2019 and TS/TC doctrine require a real risk/climate of hostility plus a "favor libertatis" reading against a group in a situation of vulnerability, and STC/ECHR doctrine gives wide latitude to harsh political criticism. So insulting a rival party will usually fail art. 510 on the merits, NOT because political ideology is unprotected. For the tracker, the usable rule is: art. 510 protected motives include ideología and aporofobia; per-politician claims must cite the actual conviction/prosecution and its cited motive, never a paraphrased scope rule from a blog.

verificationVotes.evidence:
Claim misstates the statute and is contradicted by primary sources.

1) Art. 510.1 CP's enumerated motives explicitly include "ideología": "por motivos racistas, antisemitas, antigitanos u otros referentes a la ideología, religión o creencias, situación familiar, la pertenencia de sus miembros a una etnia, raza o nación, su origen nacional, su sexo, orientación o identidad sexual, por razones de género, aporofobia, enfermedad o discapacidad". The claim's list ("race, ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation, disability") omits the one characteristic that decides the question. Political ideology is a protected motive on the face of the law (also art. 22.4 CP aggravator). Text confirmed via Iberley/BOE-indexed sources.

2) The claim's stated rationale ("covers vulnerable minorities... not political parties") is directly contradicted by Circular 7/2019 FGE (BOE-A-2019-7771), the binding prosecutorial interpretive doctrine: it states group vulnerability is NOT an element of the offence that must be proven, and expressly says that aggression against a person of Nazi ideology, or incitement to hatred against that collective, can fall within art. 510. So ideological/political groups are not categorically excluded.

3) Spain's own official record treats political ideology as a hate-motive category: Ministerio del Interior "Informe sobre la evolución de los delitos de odio en España" reports a standalone "ideología" category — 352 incidents (2023), 245 (2022), 241 (2025), ranking third. Contradicts "not political parties".

4) Source quality mismatch: a single 2021 blog post (interjuez.es) for a strong categorical statutory claim, with no cited STS/AP judgment. Even the supporting quote is weaker than the claim: it says such statements "don't constitute" art. 510 crimes, without the vulnerable-minorities-only rationale the claim adds — that rationale is an overreach layered on top of the quote.

What is defensible (but not what the claim says): calling a rival party "filofascista"/"nazis" typically fails art. 510 on freedom-of-political-expression and the required threshold (creation of a real climate of hostility/violence, direct or indirect incitement, proportionality per ECtHR/TC doctrine), plus parliamentary inviolability where applicable — not because ideology or party affiliation lies outside art. 510's protected motives.

Practical consequence for the project: a tracker cannot rely on "art. 510 excludes political groups" as a filter rule; the correct filter is the presence of an actual JEC ruling, Fiscalía case, or CENDOJ judgment.

Claim's own premise is legally false: art. 510.1.a) CP expressly lists "ideología" among the protected motives. Literal text reproduced in FGE Circular 7/2019 (BOE-A-2019-7771): "motivos racistas, antisemitas u otros referentes a la ideología, religión o creencias, situación familiar, la pertenencia de sus miembros a una etnia, raza o nación, su origen nacional, su sexo, orientación o identidad sexual, por razones de género, enfermedad o discapacidad". The claim's enumeration (race, ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation, disability) silently drops ideology — the exact ground that decides the question.

Direct contradiction of the claim's reasoning, from primary/authoritative sources:
1. FGE Circular 7/2019 (Fiscalía General del Estado, binding interpretive guidance) says "ideología" refers primarily to political conceptions of state organisation, gives ecological, feminist and labour-rights collectives as examples, and states explicitly that "una agresión a una persona de ideología nazi, o la incitación al odio hacia tal colectivo, puede ser incluida en este tipo de delitos". So a politically/ideologically defined collective is inside art. 510's scope, and the Circular states vulnerability of the group is NOT a required element of the offence — killing the claim's "vulnerable minorities only" framing.
2. STS 437/2022 (4 May 2022) upheld convictions under art. 510.2.a) CP where the discriminatory motive was the victims' political ideology (accepting Catalonia as part of Spain), and expressly distinguished art. 173.1 (any victim) from art. 510.2.a) (victim must fit an enumerated discrimination ground) — treating political ideology as one of those grounds.

Source quality mismatch: the claim is a categorical statement of criminal-law scope resting on a single 2021 blog post (interjuez.es), with no citation to the CP text, FGE circular, or Supreme Court case law. The quoted line is a conclusion about two specific epithets, from which the claim generalises to "art. 510 does not cover political parties" — an overreach beyond the quote.

Salvageable residue (not the claim as written): calling a rival party "filofascista"/"nazis" will often fail art. 510 in practice — TS jurisprudence requires creation of real risk to the protected legal interest and refuses to punish "meras expresiones de mal gusto o críticas acerbas", and political criticism is protected speech. But that is a proportionality/risk-threshold argument, not the categorical "protected characteristics exclude political parties" reason the claim asserts. For a tracker's methodology this matters: art. 510 prosecutions on ideological grounds do exist, so ideology cannot be excluded a priori from a records-based search of art. 510 cases involving politicians.

verificationVotes.evidence:
Three independent defects.

1) OVERREACH BEYOND THE QUOTE. The supporting quote states only three doctrinal attributes (absolute / perpetual / irrenunciable). The claim bolts on two propositions the quote never says: that this is "a structural bar to prosecuting many parliamentary statements" and that "no conviction record will exist for them." Neither the quantifier ("many") nor the records inference is in the source.

2) CONTRADICTED ON SCOPE — the decisive point for a politician-tracking use case. Spanish doctrine reads art. 71.1 restrictively and expressly excludes exactly the conduct such a tracker would use. Congreso's own Sinopsis of art. 71 (app.congreso.es/consti/constitucion/indice/sinopsis/sinopsis.jsp?art=71) states inviolability does not cover acts that, though occurring on the occasion of parliamentary office, have nothing to do with parliamentary functions — naming "opiniones manifestadas en declaraciones a los medios de comunicación, mítines o publicaciones" (media statements, rallies, publications). Protection runs only to opinions and votes in parliamentary acts inside the Cortes, with a narrow exception for literal reproduction outside of something said inside. So tweets, rally speeches, interviews, campaign material — the overwhelming majority of art. 510 CP hate-speech cases against Spanish politicians — are not shielded, and conviction records do exist (e.g. a Parlament de Catalunya deputy prosecuted under art. 510 over Oct 2-3 2017 tweets). "Absolute" in the doctrine means "no exception WITHIN that narrow scope", not "broad".

3) MISATTRIBUTED COURT + SOURCE QUALITY. The absolute/perpetual/irrenunciable triad is Constitutional Court doctrine, canonically STC 51/1985 (10 April 1985) — which also imposes "interpretación estricta" and grounds irrenunciabilidad in the prerogatives being institutional to the Chambers, not personal. The claim credits "the Supreme Court". Also cutting against an "absolute structural bar" framing: STC 184/2021 (28 Oct 2021) held inviolability does not shield disobeying the Constitutional Court. A single law blog (interjuez.es, 2021) is thin support for a strong doctrinal claim of this kind when the primary sources say something narrower.

Additional limit the claim ignores: art. 71.1 covers Diputados y Senadores of the Cortes Generales. Regional-parliament members' inviolability is narrower (statute-based, chamber acts only), and councillors, mayors and candidates have none — i.e. most named actors in a Spanish politician tracker are not covered at all.

Salvageable narrow core: art. 71.1 does grant inviolability for opinions in the exercise of functions, and it is described as absolute-within-scope, perpetual and non-waivable. The tracker-relevant conclusion drawn from it is wrong.

(2) It also implies an absence of public data that is wrong in substance. Art. 36 Ley 15/2022 mandates STATISTICS (binding on both FGE and CGPJ), and the Fiscalía already publishes aggregate hate-crime figures annually in the memoria chapter itself (e.g. 477 diligencias de investigación preprocesal in 2024 vs 511 in 2023) — plus Ley 15/2022 already required a hate-crime causes registry in each Fiscalía Provincial before this app. So "no registry" conflates "no unified national IT registry" with "no records/no public figures".

Whether either application actually went live in 2025 is answered by the Memoria 2026, which the claim does not consult, yet the claim is the kind of statement that would be used to assert present-day non-availability.

verificationVotes.evidence:
Claim misreads its own source and overreaches on the load-bearing part.

1) MISTRANSLATION OF "absoluta". The blog is summarising STS (Sala 2ª) of 10 Nov 2006, quoted via a TS Auto of 29 July 2021. Fetching the source page shows the SAME list also contains "Limited scope — restricted spatially and temporally to parliamentary functions" and "Completa — extends to all legal spheres (penal, civil, administrative)". So "absoluta" means the irresponsibility is total WITHIN the covered sphere, not that the covered sphere is absolute. Claim renders it "absolute in scope" and then builds "a structural bar to prosecuting many parliamentary statements" on that misreading. The source says the opposite about scope.

2) CONSTITUTIONAL DOCTRINE CONTRADICTS "absolute". STC 51/1985 holds parliamentary prerogatives negatively affect Art. 24 CE effective judicial protection and therefore admit ONLY strict/restrictive interpretation; protection "decays when acts have been realized by their author in their capacity as a citizen (or even as a politician) outside the exercise of competencies and functions" of the office. Art. 71.1 functions are not "indiscriminately all those realized by someone who is a parliamentarian". Congreso's own Sinopsis art. 71 stresses the text adds no precision beyond "opiniones manifestadas en el ejercicio de sus funciones" — i.e. it is not a general salvoconducto attached to the seat; statements to press/media fall outside.

3) THE CITED CASE WAS NOT DECIDED ON INVIOLABILITY. The 2021 TS Auto the blog analyses was dismissed on substantive art. 510 CP grounds — calling a rival party "fascistas"/"nazis" is not a hate crime because art. 510 protects social minorities (race, ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation, disability), not political parties. Inviolability was contextual dictum only. The source therefore does not evidence inviolability blocking hate-crime prosecution.

4) EMPIRICALLY FALSE THAT "no conviction record will exist" for parliamentary statements. Prosecutions over words spoken IN a plenary session do proceed: a judge sought to try a Ceuta deputy for delito de odio over "cobarde fascista" said to a Vox member in a pleno, citing SAP Valladolid 19 Jan 2021. Aforamiento only shifts competence (Fiscalía del TS instead of provincial), it does not confer inviolability. So convictions/case records for named politicians are retrievable — which is the project-relevant conclusion the claim denies.

5) SOURCE QUALITY MISMATCH. A single 2021 law blog (interjuez.es) summarising a TS Auto is being used to support a strong structural legal conclusion, with no primary citation (no CENDOJ/BOE ref for the Auto or the STS 10-11-2006) and no cross-check against STC 51/1985 or STC 243/1988, which qualify it heavily.

Salvageable core (not the claim as written): Art. 71.1 CE does grant non-waivable, post-mandate-surviving irresponsibility for opinions expressed in the exercise of parliamentary functions, and that is a real gap for statements made inside the chamber. But it is narrowly construed, does not cover rallies, press, social media or campaign material, and does not prevent conviction records for politicians' hate speech generally.

Overreach on four counts.

(1) The claim cherry-picks 3 of 5 characteristics the source itself lists. Fetching the blog (its cited authority is STS Sala 2ª of 10 Nov 2006) shows the enumeration is: absoluta, perpetua, irrenunciable, **limitada** ("restricted to parliamentary duties, spatially and temporally") and **completa**. The claim drops "limitada" — the exact feature that defeats the inference — then converts a narrow functional prerogative into "a structural bar to prosecuting many parliamentary statements." "Absolute" in that list means absolute *in kind within* parliamentary function (criminal, civil and administrative), not broad in scope.

(2) Contradicted by primary Constitutional Court doctrine. STC 243/1988 confines inviolabilidad to opinions "en actos parlamentarios y en el seno de cualquiera de las articulaciones de las Cortes Generales o, por excepción, en actos exteriores... que sean reproducción literal de un acto parlamentario", and TC doctrine requires prerogatives to be construed restrictively because they curtail art. 24 CE tutela judicial; protection "decae" for acts done by the author as a citizen. That directly conflicts with the blog's expansive "carácter ambulatorio" reading covering corridors and *electoral campaigns* — i.e. the very campaign material a tracker would look at is outside art. 71.1 on TC doctrine.

(3) Scope error fatal to the research use. Art. 71.1 CE binds only diputados/senadores of the Cortes Generales. Municipal councillors have no such prerogative and regional/city-assembly members rely on estatutos, so prosecutions do proceed: a judge processed Vox councillor Cecilia Herrero (Valencia) under arts. 510.1 and 510.2 CP with Fiscalía asking 3 years plus inhabilitación (reported 2026-05-27); a Vox councillor in Sant Adrià de Besòs faces art. 510 trial; and a Ceuta assembly deputy was proposed for trial for a hate offence over words spoken *in a plenary session*. Conviction records for politicians' hate speech therefore do exist and are retrievable — "no conviction record will exist" is false as a general proposition.

(4) The cited case does not even support the claim's mechanism: the complaint was archived under art. 313 LECrim because calling a party "filofascista"/"nazis" is not a hate crime (art. 510 CP protects social minorities, not political parties contending in elections) — a substantive ground, not inviolability.

Source quality is also insufficient for a strong structural claim: one law blog's gloss on a single 2006 Sala 2ª decision, with no BOE/CENDOJ primary text, used to override published TC jurisprudence.

verificationVotes.evidence:
Claim overreaches its own source and drops the decisive qualifier.

1. "Absolute in scope" is a misread. The blog's triad comes from STS 10 Nov 2006, where "absoluta" means it covers all acts/opinions *within* the parliamentary function — and the same source immediately states inviolability "está consiguientemente limitada, tanto espacial como temporalmente, a la función parlamentaria." So the source itself denies absolute *scope*. The claim keeps "absolute" and discards the limitation.

2. Contradicted by primary constitutional doctrine. STC 51/1985: protection "decae" when acts were performed by the author "en calidad de ciudadano —o incluso de político— fuera del ejercicio de competencias y funciones que pudieran corresponderle como parlamentario." Congress's own Sinopsis art. 71 limits the material object to opinions in parliamentary acts, plus (by exception) extra-chamber acts that are a "reproducción literal" of a parliamentary act — and the TS reads "reproducción literal" strictly, excluding amplification, clarification or explanation of what was said in the chamber. STC 184/2021 further held inviolability does not shield disobedience of the Constitutional Court. Doctrinal sources state flatly "la inviolabilidad no es absoluta."

3. The added conclusion — "a structural bar to prosecuting many parliamentary statements, meaning no conviction record will exist for them" — is not in the supporting quote and is materially misleading for the research question. Art. 71.1 CE covers only Diputados and Senadores of the Cortes Generales, not councillors, regional-parliament members or MEPs, and does not cover rallies, press conferences, party communications, campaign material or social media — precisely the record types a spending/discourse tracker would use. A live example: the Aug 2026 Fiscalía complaint against Vox deputy José María Figaredo expressly argues inviolability does not apply because the statements were made to media, not in a parliamentary session, initiative, motion or government-control act. Convictions under art. 510 CP against elected officials therefore do exist (TS has confirmed art. 510.2.a) convictions, e.g. Audiencia Provincial de Valencia, 6 months prison plus special disqualification of passive suffrage).

4. Source strength mismatch. For a strong structural claim the evidence is a private blog (interjuez.es, 2021) summarising an *Auto* (interlocutory order, TS Sala Penal, 29 July 2021) — not a sentencia — which itself quotes a 2006 STS. Primary sources (STC 51/1985, Congreso Sinopsis art. 71, STC 71/2021, STC 184/2021) qualify it heavily.

A defensible restatement would be: inviolability bars liability only for opinions in parliamentary acts (or their literal reproduction), so no judicial record exists for that narrow class of statements; everything said as citizen/politician outside that remains prosecutable.

verificationVotes.evidence:
Claim is an overreach: the quote describes CENDOJ's *institutional function* (dissemination "to citizens, the Judicial Career, public administrations and publishing companies for their reuse"), which says nothing about a legal basis for third parties to redistribute. The governing instrument says the opposite — reuse is a gatekept, licensed, fee-bearing regime.

CGPJ Reglamento 3/2010 sobre reutilización de sentencias y otras resoluciones judiciales (BOE-A-2010-17860):
- Art. 3.1 — three modalities: reuse without special conditions; reuse subject to a *type license*; reuse requiring *prior authorization* on request.
- Art. 4.1-4.2 — license-free reuse is narrow: teaching/scientific research without commercial purpose, OR fewer than 100 resolutions, occasional and informational, non-commercial.
- Art. 5.1 — any reuse outside Art. 4 "shall be subject to conditions established in standard licenses", regardless of commercial intent.
- Art. 6.1 — licensed reuse gives rise to an economic consideration in the form of a *precio público*.
- Art. 7.1-7.4 — resolutions not publicly available via CENDOJ need written prior authorization (20 days, extendable to 40).
- Art. 3.5(a) — courts are prohibited from directly supplying resolutions for reuse; access must go through CENDOJ.

Contemporaneous commentary confirms the regulation *tightened* what had previously been free: reuses formerly managed "for free and without special conditions" became subject to a license and public fee, and mass downloads / building a commercial database from the CENDOJ search engine are not permitted without following CGPJ procedures. See also HayDerecho, "Del limitado acceso a las resoluciones judiciales" (2022), which documents the restrictiveness of CENDOJ access rather than an open-reuse mandate.

Additional unaddressed constraint: the same CGPJ page states CENDOJ performs "the treatment of sentences to comply with personal data protection legislation" — i.e. content is anonymized precisely so identities are not redistributed. For the project's use case (naming living politicians and their hate-speech convictions) this cuts directly against the claim, since GDPR Art. 10 / LOPD 3/2018 and LOPJ art. 235 bis-ter govern criminal-conviction data independently of any CENDOJ dissemination mandate. A mandate to disseminate does not confer a downstream lawful basis on the redistributor.

Verdict: the source is primary and current, but it does not support the inference drawn; the actual primary norm (Reglamento 3/2010) contradicts it for anything beyond <100 resolutions or non-commercial research.

1) OVERREACH ON THE QUOTE. The cited page is a CGPJ institutional "what CENDOJ does" blurb. That is the opposite of the claim: CENDOJ/CGPJ's mandate was held NOT to reach third-party reuse. 3) NO SETTLED BASIS EXISTS TODAY. Ley 18/2015 obliged CGPJ to issue a reuse reglamento; as of 24 Apr 2025 it was still pending, and the state of play is described as "ambigua," where "algunos actores privados han podido operar con ventajas derivadas de antiguos convenios o prácticas no reguladas." The draft will impose limits, not grant freedom: "respeto al principio de anonimato de las partes," a split between free reuse and reuse "sujeta a precios públicos," plus data-protection duties. Source: https://confilegal.com/20250424-un-reglamento-marcara-el-futuro-del-acceso-a-las-sentencias-y-el-papel-de-las-editoriales-juridicas/ ; Consejo Fiscal informe on the draft: https://www.fiscal.es/documents/20142/102607/Informe+del+Consejo+Fiscal...pdf

The honour/intimidad standard is therefore the balancing test applied to a request in which interest IS alleged — it is not a special standard for interestless requesters, and no art. 4.2 pathway grants copies to someone without direct interest. Art. 5 cuts the other way still: information on the state of proceedings goes to "los interesados y quienes justifiquen interés legítimo y directo", and "Los Secretarios expedirán las certificaciones o los testimonios de las actuaciones judiciales no declaradas secretas ni reservadas a las partes que se soliciten" — i.e. certifications/testimonios to the PARTIES, with art. 5 expressly subject to the art. 4.2 criteria. Art. 4.1 likewise frames the duty as facilitating access "a los interesados". Two further defects: (1) denial/silence is reviewable by the Juez within three days (art. 4.3), so the Secretario is not the final standard-setter the claim implies; (2) the office title is outdated — "Secretario Judicial" was renamed "Letrado de la Administración de Justicia" by LO 7/2015, so a live-law statement about "the standard the Secretario must apply" is stale terminology. Verified against the consolidated primary text at BOE-A-2005-15939 (Reglamento 1/2005 CGPJ, aspectos accesorios de las actuaciones judiciales), vigente, "Última actualización" 20/02/2025 (further modified by Acuerdo de 12 de febrero de 2025). Art. 4.2 verbatim: the request "será resuelta ... mediante acuerdo del Secretario de la unidad de la Oficina judicial ..., quien deberá valorar si el solicitante justifica su interés, la existencia de derechos fundamentales en juego, y la necesidad de tratar los documentos a exhibir o de omitir datos de carácter personal en los testimonios o certificaciones a expedir, en caso de que el solicitante no justifique un interés personal y directo, de manera que se salvaguarde el derecho a la intimidad personal y familiar, al honor y a la propia imagen de los afectados por la resolución judicial."

Element-by-element: (a) the trigger condition is expressly lack of "interés personal y directo" — matches the claim's "requesters without direct interest"; (b) the addressee is the Secretario (now Letrado de la Administración de Justicia; the consolidated text still says "Secretario" in art. 4.2) — matches; (c) the stated standard is verbatim "intimidad personal y familiar, al honor y a la propia imagen" — matches the supporting quote exactly; (d) art. 5 closes the loop for issued documents: certificaciones/testimonios are expedited "con sujeción, en su caso, a los criterios establecidos en el artículo 4.2 de este Reglamento." No source found disputing or qualifying the provision's existence or wording.

Three qualifications that do not defeat the claim: (1) the operative duty is to assess redaction/"tratamiento" of personal data, with the honour/privacy triad as the express purpose clause — so the triad is the governing standard teleologically, not a free-standing veto; (2) "LO 1/1982-style" is loose labelling — the triad is the art. 18.1 CE wording that LO 1/1982 develops civilly, so the reglamento echoes the constitutional right, not the 1982 statute's regime (still, the claim's substantive point that honour protection sits inside the CGPJ access rule itself is correct); (3) the art. 5 final paragraph on "copias simples de escritos y documentos" carries no express cross-reference to art. 4.2, so for plain copies specifically the anchoring is weaker than for testimonios/certificaciones. Also note scope limit for downstream use: art. 4.2 governs third-party ACCESS to case documents, not the lawfulness of republishing a named person's conviction (that runs through LOPJ arts. 235 bis/ter, Reglamento 3/2018 CGPJ and GDPR art. 10).
